Imaging predictors of adverse outcome
Morpho-functional parameters

The MLVWT was associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 1.17 per mm increase; 95% CI: 1.09-1.25; p < .001; seven studies, I 2 = 73.5%) and with the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 1.19 per mm increase, 95% CI: 1.04-1.36, p = .01; five studies, I 2 = 87.7%).

The LVMI was associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 1.02 per mg/m2 increase; 95% CI: 1.01-1.02; p < .001; seven studies, I 2 = 75.4%) and with the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 1.01 per mg/m2 increase; 95% CI: 1.00-1.02; p < .001; five studies, I 2 = 56.7%).

The LV-GLS was associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 1.22 per unit increase; 95% CI: 1.17-1.27; p < .001; five studies, I 2 = 0%) and with the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 1.20 per unit increase; 95% CI: 1.16-1.25; p < .001; five studies, I 2 = 0%).

The LAVI was not associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 1.03 per mL/m2 increase; 95% CI: 0.98-1.08; p = .19; four studies, I 2 = 93%); however, it was significantly associated with the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 1.02 per mL/m2 increase; 95% CI: 1.01-1.03; p < .001; three studies; I 2 = 0.2%).
The LVEF was not associated with any of the two endpoints (HR: 0.96 per unit increase; 95% CI: 0.90-1.03; p = .30; five studies, I 2 = 82.3% for both endpoints).
The E/e' was significantly associated with both the composite and the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 1.14 per unit increase; 95% CI: 1.08-1.21; p < .001; two studies, I 2 = 0% for both endpoints).
Tissue abnormalities

Native-T1 was significantly associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 0.99 per msec increase; 95% CI: 0.98-1.00; p = .01; three studies, I 2 = 71.3%); however, significance was lost when assessing the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 0.99; 95% CI: 0.97-1.00; p = .11; two studies, I 2 = 85.4%).

Native-T2 was not associated with the composite endpoint (HR: 1.16 per msec increase; 95% CI: 0.94-1.43; p = .16; three studies, I 2 = 82%). The cardiovascular endpoint could not be assessed due to insufficient number of studies.

The presence of LGE was significantly associated with an increased risk for the composite endpoint (HR: 3.56; 95% CI: 1.73-7.34; p = .001; six studies, I 2 = 62.9%) and an even higher risk for the cardiovascular endpoint (HR: 4.45; 95% CI: 2.82-7.02; p < .001; six studies, I 2 = 9%). The relevant forest plots are shown in Figures 2 and 3. When Tao et al., the only studied classified as poor quality, was excluded from the analysis, there was no substantial change in the results with respect to both endpoints.

Meta-regression analysis

A meta-regression analysis did not show any significant interaction between age, % of males, proportion of patients receiving ERT, prevalence of LGE, LVMI, follow-up duration, type of variant and any of the two endpoints.
Subgroup analysis

A subgroup analysis was performed, by analysing separately TTE and CMR-derived parameters for the two endpoints whenever the number of studies was sufficiently large for single imaging predictor and excluding Reant et al. which did not specify the imaging modality for some of the parameters. The results did not diverge significantly from the main analysis and are shown in Table S5.
Publication bias and grading of evidence

The certainty of evidence between the effect of single imaging parameters and the evaluated endpoints is shown in Tables S6 and S7. Asymmetry tests indicated possible bias for MLVWT with respect to the composite endpoint (p < .05). For all other single imaging parameters included, the meta-analysis diagnostics showed no significant concerns of 'small study effects' or publication bias with respect to the composite and cardiovascular endpoints, although a degree of asymmetry was graphically present in a few comparison-specific funnel plots (Figures S1 and S2).
DISCUSSION

In this meta-analysis of 14 independent studies, we provide pooled adjusted estimates of the prognostic value of cardiovascular imaging parameters, both CMR- and echocardiography-derived, in more than 1700 patients with FD cardiomyopathy.

Risk stratification in patients with FD is key in view of the availability of disease-specific therapies and the need for tailored clinical decision-making. Several imaging parameters serve as non-invasive markers unveiling FD cardiac involvement. Considering that cardiovascular mortality represents the main cause of death in this population, such imaging parameters are potential non-invasive harbingers of adverse outcomes. However, current evidence is bounded by the small sample sizes of individual studies, the paucity of clinical events and the absence of multimodality imaging assessment at baseline. A systematic review and meta-analysis of current literature is therefore needed to establish whether and which cardiac imaging features have a prognostic value for FD patients.
Morpho-functional parameters

In the late stages, FD cardiomyopathy is a phenocopy of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and a model of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Myocardial hypertrophy reflects the storage of glycosphingolipids in all cardiac cellular types triggering secondary damage pathways of inflammation and fibrosis, resulting in increased MLVWT and LV mass. Advanced stages of FD cardiomyopathy are characterized by overt LVH and unfavourable clinical outcomes. LVH might represent a balanced combination of sphingolipid accumulation and myocyte hypertrophy in females, whereas in males LVH could mainly reflect myocyte hypertrophy triggered by Gb3 accumulation. The present meta-analysis demonstrates that the risk of adverse outcomes parallels the degree of MLVWT and the amount of LV mass, independently from sex expression at meta-regression analysis. Notably, CMR is more accurate than TTE in measuring LV mass and MLVWT because it is not dependent on acoustic windows and directly quantifies LV mass, regardless of mathematical assumptions, and it considers LV trabeculae and papillary muscles, which are abnormally increased in FD.

LVH is a determinant of diastolic dysfunction and increased LV filling pressures testified by increased E/e', which showed a significant association with adverse outcomes in our analysis. Consistently, LAVI, which is an indirect marker of diastolic dysfunction, showed an association with cardiovascular outcomes. Interestingly, atrial remodelling may precede LVH in FD patients due to local Gb3 accumulation, representing an early and prognostically useful marker of cardiac involvement.

In patients with FD, LVEF is typically preserved until the very-late stages, when myocardial fibrosis becomes extensive; it may thus not be a sensitive prognostic marker to risk-stratify patients with shorter disease course. Accordingly, LVEF was not associated with adverse prognosis at our analysis. Conversely, less negative values of LV-GLS were associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes, supporting a well-grounded place for strain imaging as a risk-stratifier in FD patients. Spinelli et al. found that LV-GLS was significantly correlated with LVH, but reduced GLS values have been found also in the pre-hypertrophy phase allowing early diagnosis of FD cardiomyopathy.
Tissue abnormalities

A unique advantage of CMR is the capability to provide non-invasive tissue characterization, including Gb3 storage as well as myocardial fibrosis and inflammation, which have been respectively associated with lower native-T1 mapping values and LGE. We found a significant association between low native-T1 values and the composite clinical endpoint; however, we did not confirm this result regarding the cardiovascular endpoint. By including only native-T1 values measured in the septum, we prevented looking at 'pseudonormalized' T1 values typically occurring in the inferolateral wall because of myocardial fibrosis, leading to increased regional and global myocardial T1. The initiation of ERT guided by early organ involvement, as recommended by current guidelines, may contribute to explain the lack of association between low T1-values and the cardiovascular endpoint. Our data align with these recommendations and allow us to hypothesize that early ERT may be effective in protecting from cardiovascular outcomes by preventing myocardial fibrosis and inflammation. In fact, Gb3 storage is a very early sign of myocardial involvement, potentially preceding by years the development of inflammation and fibrosis, which in turn might be the true determinant of adverse outcomes. Accordingly, we found that the presence of LGE, regardless of its location and extension, constituted a strong prognostic factor, conveying a more than three times higher risk of composite adverse outcome and a more than four times higher risk of cardiovascular adverse outcome. Importantly, although LGE is usually a feature of advanced FD cardiomyopathy, women may present LGE before LVH development. It should be mentioned that the prognostic value of LGE was not affected by sex, as shown by the meta-regression analysis. This observation together with our data on LGE enhance once more the central role of CMR for FD patients, especially in the early stages of the disease, to refine risk stratification. For the same purpose, in the future it will be necessary to investigate more in deep the value of LGE extent in this population, considering that recent findings suggest a prognostic role for this parameter in several cardiomyopathies, and that up to 50% of FD patients have some degree of LGE at CMR.

Recently, T2-mapping has been claimed to represent another biomarker of FD-related inflammation, being associated with troponin release. We did not observe a significant association between T2-mapping and adverse clinical outcomes, but it is essential to remind that only three studies were available for pooled analysis. Moreover, there were substantial methodological discrepancies among the studies. Overall, our data call for further prospective studies assessing the prognostic value of this novel imaging parameter in FD.
Clinical implications

The observation that the prognostic value of both morpho-functional and tissutal parameters was not modified by the proportion of patients undergoing ERT could suggest that the prognostic value of such parameters is maintained after ERT initiation or, vice versa, that ERT does not protect from established cardiac involvement calling for early diagnosis and timely ERT initiation based on early markers, such as LV-GLS, diastolic dysfunction and/or left atrial enlargement.

Osborne et al. recently developed a risk prediction model, including age, T1-dispersion and LVMI at CMR to predict 5-year adverse cardiac outcomes in a cohort of FD patients. Meucci et al. proposed a staging classification of FD patients where the extent of myocardial involvement, evaluated through simple echocardiographic parameters, such as the presence of LVH, left atrium enlargement and/or ventricular impairment, strongly and incrementally associates with prognosis. Collectively, these studies suggest that risk stratification should rely on the integration of multiple imaging tools. Our meta-analysis confirms and expands these results, encouraging future longitudinal studies focusing on comprehensive multimodality imaging assessment to build up potentially more precise algorithms to early intercept patients at risk of adverse trajectories.
Limitations

Our meta-analysis has a few limitations. First, we included only observational studies, which have an intrinsic risk for selection bias. Second, the included studies presented significant heterogeneity with respect to patient populations and ERT, and some studies did not specify the proportion of patients with classic and late-onset phenotypes. However, several meta-regression analyses confirm the robustness of our data. Third, methods of calculating LV mass (i.e. inclusion vs. exclusion of papillary muscles/trabeculations), evaluating LGE (i.e. number of SD set to adjudicate presence of LGE) and T2-mapping (i.e. septum vs. basal inferolateral wall) varied across studies. Fourth, TTE- and CMR-derived morpho-functional parameters (i.e. LV-GLS, LAVI, LVEF, MLVWT and LVMI) and two-dimensional and three-dimensional GLS were pooled together despite methodological differences due to the low number of individual studies; however, the reported agreement between the two is strong. Fifth, as this is a study-level meta-analysis, partially overlapping samples of patients cannot be excluded. A final limitation concerns the complexity of the combined clinical endpoints considered, precluding granular risk stratification for specific outcomes. This flaw reflects the limitations of the existing literature influenced by the low rate of adverse cardiac events in FD patients nowadays.
CONCLUSIONS

This meta-analysis demonstrates a robust prognostic value regarding several imaging parameters in FD, specifically indexes of LV mass and wall thickness, diastolic function, LV-GLS and LGE presence. The latter showed the strongest association with adverse clinical outcomes. These findings support multimodality cardiovascular imaging in FD patients to predict long-term prognosis; however, as it emerged from the present work, considerable variability exists in present-day studies of FD regarding endpoint definition and imaging protocols. Multicentre collaborative efforts are needed employing standardized data collection protocols, such as the new Italian Fabry Disease Cardiovascular Registry, to harmonize and validate existing and emerging imaging biomarkers.

passages.text: A Golgi apparatus-related subtype and risk signature predicts prognosis and evaluates immunotherapy response in gastric cancer
Background

Gastric cancer (GC) remains a significant health burden, calling for the discovery of novel biomarkers. Golgi apparatus, a crucial cellular organelle involved in tumorigenesis, remains underexplored in GC research. A comprehensive understanding of its role and associated mechanisms is urgently needed.
Materials and methods

Utilizing the TCGA-STAD dataset as the training cohort and GSE84433 as the validation cohort, we explored potential associations between Golgi apparatus-related genes (GARG) and GC clinical risk. We aimed to decipher the prognostic significance and underlying biological mechanisms of these genes via consistent clustering, differential expression analysis, enrichment analyses, and immune infiltration profiling. To assess the relationship between risk stratification and survival outcomes, drug sensitivity, and immune infiltration, we developed the Golgi Apparatus-Related Risk Signature (GARRS). The reliability of GARRS was further corroborated using immunohistochemical staining.
Results

Consensus clustering based on 17 GARG identified two patient subgroups, C1 and C2, exhibiting differential survival, immune scores, and immune cell infiltration. We developed a GARRS using Cox-Lasso regression analysis, accurately stratifying patients into high- and low-risk groups. GARRS' validity was confirmed in the validation set and immunohistochemical staining. Our findings underline the Golgi apparatus' significance in the GC immune microenvironment and GARRS' utility in predicting GC survival outcomes.
Conclusion

This study underscores the association between Golgi apparatus subtypes and GC immunotumor microenvironment. GARRS, validated for its prognostic, immune infiltration, and drug sensitivity predictive abilities, offers new insights into gastric cancer treatment strategies.
Introduction

Gastric cancer (GC) is one of the leading causes of cancer mortality worldwide, often resulting in delayed diagnosis due to nonspecific early symptoms, leading to poor prognosis. Although surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy are common treatment modalities, GC prognosis remains unsatisfactory despite recent diagnostic and therapeutic advancements. Therefore, urgently needed are effective biomarkers and prognostic models to improve GC patient outcomes.

The Golgi apparatus, serving as a hub for intracellular transport, synthesis, and modification, is pivotal in biological processes like protein synthesis and localization. Recent studies suggest a strong linkage between Golgi dysfunction and the pathogenesis of diverse diseases, encompassing degenerative conditions, cardiovascular ailments, and cancer.

While the Golgi apparatus is thought to play a significant role in tumorigenesis, its prognostic features have been established in cancers like breast, thyroid, hepatocellular, and head and neck carcinomas. Its role and related mechanisms in gastric cancer (GC), however, remain unexplored and deserve further investigation.

annotations.text: breast, thyroid, hepatocellular, and head and neck carcinomas

passages.text: In this study, we introduce the Golgi apparatus-related risk signature (GARRS), a novel biomarker to predict gastric cancer (GC) prognosis. We also explored GARRS' application in evaluating patients' immunotherapeutic sensitivity. GARRS' validity in assessing GC patients' immune microenvironment and survival prognosis holds promise for novel therapeutic targets, facilitating precision medicine.
Materials and methods
Data sources

Transcriptome data from 407 STAD cases, including 375 STAD samples and 32 normal samples, were retrieved from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA, https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/). Mutation and associated clinicopathological information were also retrieved for the training set. For the validation set, microarray gene chips from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/, accession: GSE84433, platform: GPL6947) were used, containing data from 357 patients.
Consensus clustering analysis of Golgi-related subtypes

We identified 21 Golgi-related genes, including BSTIP1, PLOD3, LLGL1, AP3M2, DENND4B, ARHGEF2, RHBDF2, VPS45, GALNT10, GLA, SORT1, SIPA1L3, RNF24, ABCC5, SCAMP3, BSG, BCL9, RUSC1, GAL3ST1, PKMYT1, and KIF20A, for our study.

ConsensusClusterPlus was applied to aggregate km clusters for cluster analysis using 1-log correlation distance, resampling 80% of samples 10 times. We determined the optimal number of clusters by evaluating the AUC of the consistent cumulative distribution function, K-value, and within-group consistency to ensure stability.
Identification and analysis of differentially expressed genes

Utilising the R package limma (version 3.40.6), we identified differential genes (DEGs) between various groups in this study, applying a stringent criterion of adjusted p < 0.05 and lfold changel> 1.5. Following this, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses to compare the differential signalling pathways and biological effects across the distinct Golgi apparatus-related cluster cohorts. These enrichment analyses were based on a stringent threshold of q-value and p-value < 0.05.
Mutation landscape analysis
We obtained somatic mutation data from TCGA for STAD patients to assess genetic structural differences between groups and visualised mutant genes using waterfall plots.
Construction and validation of GARRS

LASSO, a regression analysis technique, combines variable selection and regularization to enhance the predictive accuracy and interpretability of statistical models. In this study, the R package glmnet was used to perform LASSO-Cox regression analysis, integrating survival time, status, and gene expression data. Optimal model selection was achieved through tenfold cross-validation. Additionally, a nomogram was developed to predict 1-, 3-, and 5 year survival outcomes for GC patients, incorporating TNM classification, age, gender, and risk characteristics.
Immune cell infiltration analysis

Using the CIBERSORT algorithm, we evaluated the relative proportions of 22 immune cells. Differences in estimated scores, immune scores, and stromal scores were determined using the ESTIMATE algorithm. Additionally, the Spearman correlation test was performed to assess correlations between risk scores and immune cells.
Drug sensitivity analysis

We evaluated the response to chemotherapeutic and immunological drugs by analyzing the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values. Using the R package "pRRophetic," we predicted the IC50 of various drugs in GC samples, assessing the association between high- and low-risk groups and drug sensitivity.
Immunohistochemical validation of Golgi-associated prognostic genes

Data on immunohistochemical staining of both gastric cancer (GC) and normal tissues were obtained from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA; http://www.proteinatlas.org/). At the protein expression level, prognostic genes related to the Golgi apparatus were validated. The staining intensity was graded as high, intermediate, low, or not detected. Furthermore, overall survival curves for GC patients were derived.
Result
Distinct Golgi apparatus-related subtypes were identified through cluster analysis

Identification of Golgi apparatus-related subtypes by consensus clustering. A Heatmap of the expression of 21 Golgi apparatus-related genes in GC samples, including tumour and normal samples; (B, C) Cluster analysis of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) indicating the area under the curve and the decreasing trend of Delta at k = 2-10 and the decreasing trend of area under the curve and Delta; (D) Example cluster consistency plot showing that the consensus value is optimal when k = 2; (E) Heatmap of Golgi apparatus-related gene expression in the 2 subtypes; (F) Consensus matrix for optimal k = 2; (G) Kaplan-Meier curves (p = 0.02)

The study examined gene expression patterns of Golgi apparatus genes in normal and gastric cancer (GC) tissues. Results showed that GC samples had significantly higher expression levels of Golgi apparatus genes compared to normal tissues, as depicted in Fig. 1A. This suggests a potential role of the Golgi apparatus in GC development.

Identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and functional enrichment analysis of biological pathways between two Golgi-apparatus subtypes. A Volcano plot showing two groups of Golgi apparatus-related DEGs; (B) heatmap showing DEG expression between the 2 isoforms; (C, D) bubble plots showing enrichment of potential signalling pathways for GO and KEGG

A comprehensive analysis was conducted on 375 gastric cancer samples to explore the relationship between Golgi apparatus gene expression and patient survival. The findings revealed two distinct subtypes (referred to as C1 and C2) based on gene expression patterns in the Golgi apparatus. The consensus matrix, optimized at K = 2, provided a clear visualization of these subtypes (see Fig. 1B-D). Further examination showed that patients belonging to subtype C1 exhibited a significantly better clinical outcome compared to those in subtype C2 (P = 0.02), as illustrated in the Kaplan-Meier survival curve (Fig. 1G). These results highlight the potential impact of Golgi apparatus gene expression on patient prognosis, offering valuable insights for personalized treatment strategies in gastric cancer management Fig. 2.
Differential gene expression analyzed in Golgi apparatus subtypes, revealing enriched functions and pathways

The research aimed to uncover the molecular mechanisms that underlie the varying prognostic outcomes of the two distinct Golgi apparatus subtypes. Through an analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) within each subtype, a total of 525 up-regulated DEGs and 455 down-regulated DEGs were identified, showcasing significant variations in their expression levels. These findings provided valuable insight into the biological foundations that set the subtypes apart. Further exploration through GO and KEGG enrichment analyses highlighted the association of these DEGs with crucial processes such as cell cycle regulation, cell proliferation, and cancer-related pathways. Specifically, the DEGs were found to be linked with activities like cell cycle progression, stimulus response regulation, and involvement in signaling pathways related to cancer and viral infections. These discoveries shed light on the potential roles played by these DEGs in influencing diverse disease states.
Comparing mutations, tumor environment, and immune checkpoints in Golgi-related subtypes reveals unique characteristics that affect cancer progression

In the study, somatic mutations were examined in patients from two different groups, leading to the creation of a waterfall plot showcasing the top 15 genes with the highest mutation frequency. Notably, group C1 displayed mutations in genes such as TTN, TP53, MUC16, SYNE1, and LRP1B. However, in group C2, CSMD3 emerged as a key player with a mutation frequency of 30.3%, surpassing that of group C1 at 25.8%. Strikingly, TTN and TP53 mutation frequencies were notably lower in group C2 (51.6, 45.1%) compared to group C1 (59.4, 53.9%). These findings shed light on the distinct genetic landscape present in each group, underscoring the importance of further research in this field.

Somatic mutations and immune infiltration in 2 Golgi apparatus subtypes. A, B Mutation map waterfall plot showing the 15 most common mutated genes in GC differing between groups C1 and C2; (C) ESTIMATE box-and-line plot showing the IMMUNE SCORE, STOMAL SCORE and ESTIMATE SCORE of the infiltrating different subtypes; (D) Box-and-line plot showing the expression difference of some of the immune checkpoints in 2 Golgi apparatus subtypes; (E) CIBERSORT box-and-line plot showing the differences in the infiltration of 22 immune cells between the 3 Golgi apparatus subtypes *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001

A study comparing the tumour microenvironment in two subtypes revealed intriguing findings. Results indicated that the C2 group exhibited higher levels of immune score, stromal score, and estimated score compared to the C1 group (Fig. 3C). Furthermore, analysis of immune checkpoints demonstrated that the majority were expressed at higher levels in the C1 group (Fig. 3D). These results have significant implications, suggesting that immunotherapy may be more beneficial for patients in the C1 group. This study sheds light on potential treatment strategies tailored to different subtypes of tumours.

The CIBERSORT method was employed to analyze immune cell infiltration in two groups, revealing distinct patterns. Activated CD4 + memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, M0 macrophages, and M1 macrophages showed higher infiltration in group C1 compared to group C2. Conversely, resting CD4 + memory T cells, M2 macrophages, and resting Mast cells exhibited the opposite trend. This data, visualized using a box-and-line plot, highlights significant differences in immune cell composition between the two groups, shedding light on potential underlying mechanisms impacting immune responses.
A new risk signature based on Golgi apparatus shows potential for predicting health outcomes

Our study utilized survival time, survival status, and gene expression data to conduct regression analyses employing the lasso-cox method. By setting Lambda at 0.0521746172425181, we identified 17 Golgi apparatus-related prognostic genes. These genes include SLC52A3, RGS2, GJA1, SNORC, SLC39A4, SP6, BATF2, APOD, CTSV, FP671120.4, SST, ENTPD2, GPX3, BEX3, DDC, MAGEA3, and MMP11. The calculated model equations further revealed the impact of each gene on the RiskScore, shedding light on their individual contributions to the prognosis.

The study focused on analyzing the connection between survival rates and risk scores, revealing a notable correlation between the two. It was observed that as the risk score increased, patient survival decreased significantly. Several genes, including RGS2, GJA1, APOD, GPX3, and BEX3, were pinpointed as risk factors, showing an increase in expression as the risk score rose. Conversely, genes such as SLC52A3, SNORC, SP6, ENTPD2, and DDC were identified as protective factors, exhibiting a decrease in expression with higher risk scores. By evaluating the GARRS via Kaplan-Meier analysis, it was found that the low-risk group displayed a more favorable survival prognosis, both in the TCGA-STAD cohort and the GSE84433 validation set. These results indicate that the GARRS developed during the study demonstrates strong predictive performance in identifying patient outcomes.
GARRS association with prognosis is significant in medical research

A comprehensive study utilizing multifactorial Cox analysis revealed that the GARRS serves as an independent prognostic indicator for overall survival in gastric cancer (GC) patients. In addition to this discovery, a nomogram was created using TNM classification, age, gender, and risk features to enhance prognostic accuracy. The nomogram was validated through calibration curves, which depicted a strong alignment between predicted and actual GC survival rates. Furthermore, ROC analysis yielded favorable AUC values of 0.76, 0.80, and 0.82 for 1, 3, and 5 years, respectively, underscoring the reliability of the Golgi apparatus-related risk score in predicting GC patient survival. These encouraging results highlight the potential of GARRS in improving prognostic assessments and guiding treatment decisions for GC patients.
GARRS' relationship with tumor environment and drug response influences treatment outcomes significantly

The immune microenvironment's dynamics are influenced by GARG, specifically GARRS. Analyzing their impact, we found a direct relationship between the GARRS risk score and the infiltrating immune cells. Our results show a positive correlation between the level of risk and the abundance of M2 macrophages and resting mast cells. Conversely, a negative correlation was noted with T follicular helper cells and resting NK cells. This correlation pattern was consistent in the validation set GSE84433. These findings shed light on the complex interplay between GARG and immune cell infiltration in the microenvironment.

After analyzing the predictive values of IC50 in both high and low-risk groups, we identified 16 compounds that showed varying levels of drug sensitivity for each group. The results of the drug sensitivity analysis revealed that patients in the low-risk group responded better to certain inhibitors, including Src family Lck inhibitor (A-770041), AKT inhibitor VIII, Ponatinib (AP-24534), Saracatinib (AZD-0530), PLK1 inhibitor (BI-2536), Dasatinib, Wnt/beta-catenin and PPAR inhibitors (FH535), and B-RafV600E inhibitor (PLX4720). On the other hand, patients in the high-risk group showed increased sensitivity to Veliparib (ABT-888), Chk inhibitor (AZD7762), Afatinib (BIBW2992), ATM-specific inhibitor (KU-55933), Methotrexate, Linsitinib (OSI-906), Parthenolide, and Vinblastine. These findings have the potential to guide personalized medication strategies tailored to the specific needs of each group.
Golgi apparatus-related proteins validated for improved prognosis prediction, enhancing medical research accuracy

Our study aimed to explore the biological functions of prognostic genes in Gastric Adenocarcinoma with Refractory Stomachs (GARRS) and Gastric Cancer (GC) by examining the protein expression levels of Golgi apparatus-related prognostic genes. Through analysis of Human Protein Atlas immunohistochemical staining data, we found that APOD, BEX3, and GJA1 were significantly elevated in GC tissues, while ENTPD2, SLC52A3, and SNORC were decreased, confirming our previous findings. Unfortunately, we were unable to obtain validated data for other genes. These results suggest that these markers, particularly APOD, BEX3 and GJA1, play a crucial role in the development of gastric cancer. The newly developed GARRS may serve as a more precise tool in predicting potential prognostic and therapeutic markers for gastric cancer, offering new insights into the disease and its treatment.
Discussion

Gastric cancer (GC) continues to pose a significant threat to global health, being one of the most critical digestive system malignancies. Scientists have been dedicatedly investigating potential biological markers that could predict or improve patient outcomes in GC. Recent research has shed light on the correlation between dysfunction of the golgi apparatus and the development and advancement of GC, offering new perspectives on the treatment of this cancer. Despite these findings, the precise role of the golgi apparatus in GC, as well as the underlying mechanisms and pathways involved, remain largely unknown.

In our research, we delved into the intricacies of the Golgi apparatus, a cellular organelle crucial for protein processing and trafficking, by analyzing the gene expression patterns of 21 GARG. Through meticulous consensus clustering, we were able to categorize patients with gastric cancer (GC) into two distinct subgroups based on their Golgi apparatus profiles. What truly astounded us was the profound impact these differences had on patient survival, immune cell infiltration levels, and overall prognosis. The findings, showcased in Figs. 1G and 3, shed light on the intricate interplay between molecular subtypes of GC and clinical outcomes.Utilizing cutting-edge statistical methods such as limma and cox-lasso, we honed in on 17 specific genes that were differentially expressed between the two identified subgroups. These genes, when combined, formed the basis of our novel prognostic tool:the GARRS. Among these genes, APOD, BEX3, SLC52A3, and ENTPD2 stood out as key players in cancer progression and immune modulation. APOD, for instance, was found to regulate oxidative stress and inflammation, while targeting BEX3 showed promise in overcoming drug resistance in cancer cells. The abnormal expression of SLC52A3 is related to the progressive development of esophageal cancer and the survival rate of patients. Overexpression of ENTPD2 is considered to be an indicator of poor prognosis of HCC, and ENTPD2 inhibitors can reduce the growth of cancer cells and improve the efficiency and efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Our study underscored the critical role of GARG in shaping the tumor microenvironment and influencing patient outcomes. By targeting these specific genes, we may pave the way for more effective treatment strategies and improved prognostic assessments in GC and potentially other cancers Figs. 4 and 5.

The study on 17 specific genes indicated that our GARRS led to improved survival rates in low-risk patients, as demonstrated in both the initial and validation data. These findings highlight a promising treatment approach that may involve influencing the tumor microenvironment. The potential impact of GARRS on patient prognosis is significant and merits further investigation.

The analysis of our CIBERSORT box plot revealed significant differences in the immune cell infiltration between two distinct groups, C1 and C2. The C1 group exhibited higher levels of activated CD4 + memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, M0 macrophages, and M1 macrophages compared to the C2 group. Conversely, resting CD4 + memory T cells, M2 macrophages, and resting Mast cells showed lower infiltration in the C1 group. Memory CD4 + T cells play a critical role in mounting a rapid and robust immune response, essential for maintaining protective immunity. T follicular helper cells provide crucial support for B cell immune responses. M1 macrophages are involved in killing bacteria and pathogens through the release of inflammatory molecules, while M2 macrophages aid in anti-inflammatory responses and tissue repair processes. The increased immune cell infiltration observed in the C1 group may contribute to better survival outcomes in gastric cancer patients. Furthermore, the higher expression of immune checkpoints in the C1 group suggests that immunotherapy may be more effective for patients in this subgroup, aligning with the previous findings. Overall, the data underscores the importance of understanding the complex interactions between immune cell subtypes and their impact on patient outcomes in gastric cancer.

The significance of GARG in the immune microenvironment was the focal point of our investigation. By delving deeper into the relationship between GARRS and immune cell infiltration, we discovered compelling correlations that shed light on potential implications for gastric cancer prognosis and treatment. Our findings revealed a positive association between the risk score and the infiltration of M2 macrophages and resting Mast cells, while a negative correlation was observed with T follicular helper cells and resting NK cells (see Fig. 6A-D). This pattern of association was further validated in the GSE84433 verification set (see Fig. 6E-H).Moreover, our exploration led to the identification of 16 compounds that exhibited differential sensitivity between high and low-risk groups based on predicted IC50 values. Interestingly, each group showed heightened sensitivity to 8 unique compounds, suggesting the possibility of individualized medication strategies for patients based on their risk score (refer to Fig. 7). Additionally, we evaluated the protein expression levels of Golgi apparatus-related prognostic genes in normal tissues and GC using HPA immunohistochemical staining data, revealing their potential significance in gastric cancer.In summary, our study underscores the utility of GARRS in predicting prognosis and therapeutic markers for gastric cancer with enhanced precision. These insights emphasize the importance of considering the immune microenvironment and GARG in advancing personalized treatments for patients with gastric cancer Fig. 8.
Limitations and future direction

While bioinformatics analysis is a valuable tool for accurate data analysis and prediction of potential biomarkers, this study also has its limitations that need to be addressed. In the future, we aim to confirm our findings through experimental methods such as real-time PCR and western blot in cell and animal studies, including the incorporation of knockout or overexpression experiments to explore the molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it is crucial to validate the results of this paper in other gastric cancer cohorts to ensure the reliability and generalizability of the findings. Furthermore, as this study is retrospective, it is essential to conduct further prospective, multi-center studies to validate the results. By addressing these limitations and incorporating a variety of research methods, we can enhance the robustness and applicability of our findings in the field of gastric cancer research.
Conclusion

Our research emphasizes the impact of Golgi apparatus-related subtypes on the immune tumor microenvironment in gastric cancer. We have developed a GARRS that has useful in predicting survival rates, immune system infiltration, and drug responsiveness in gastric cancer patients. These findings advance our comprehension of the Golgi apparatus.

passages.text: Tuberculosis vaccines and therapeutic drug: challenges and future directions

Tuberculosis (TB) remains a prominent global health challenge, with the World Health Organization documenting over 1 million annual fatalities. Despite the deployment of the Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine and available therapeutic agents, the escalation of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains underscores the pressing need for more efficacious vaccines and treatments. This review meticulously maps out the contemporary landscape of TB vaccine development, with a focus on antigen identification, clinical trial progress, and the obstacles and future trajectories in vaccine research. We spotlight innovative approaches, such as multi-antigen vaccines and mRNA technology platforms. Furthermore, the review delves into current TB therapeutics, particularly for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), exploring promising agents like bedaquiline (BDQ) and delamanid (DLM), as well as the potential of host-directed therapies. The hurdles in TB vaccine and therapeutic development encompass overcoming antigen diversity, enhancing vaccine effectiveness across diverse populations, and advancing novel vaccine platforms. Future initiatives emphasize combinatorial strategies, the development of anti-TB compounds targeting novel pathways, and personalized medicine for TB treatment and prevention. Despite notable advances, persistent challenges such as diagnostic failures and protracted treatment regimens continue to impede progress. This work aims to steer future research endeavors toward groundbreaking TB vaccines and therapeutic agents, providing crucial insights for enhancing TB prevention and treatment strategies.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s43556-024-00243-6.
Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be a leading cause of infectious disease-related mortality worldwide, with the World Health Organization's 2023 Global Tuberculosis Report estimating 1.3 million TB-related deaths in 2022. Globally, over 10 million new cases of active TB are reported annually, highlighting the disease's ongoing public health challenge. In high-burden countries like China, which reported 748,000 new cases and 30,000 deaths in 2022, TB remains a significant concern due to its widespread prevalence and the emergence of drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB).

Vaccination has been proven to be one of the most cost-effective public health strategies, playing a crucial role in achieving the World Health Organization's (WHO) global strategy to end TB by 2035. Currently, the Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine remains the only approved vaccine for TB prevention. Despite its critical role in reducing severe TB in infants and children, BCG's limited efficacy in preventing adult pulmonary TB and its ineffectiveness against primary or latent TB infection highlight the urgent need for more effective vaccines. With the continuous exploration and in-depth research in TB vaccinology, numerous new vaccine candidates are currently in various stages of clinical trials, while many more are at the preclinical stage. The primary aim is to either replace the BCG vaccine or to enhance its efficacy through a prime-boost immunization strategy. Furthermore, recent advances in bioinformatics and artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly transformed vaccine research, particularly in the identification of novel MTB antigens and vaccine targets. AI can be used in antigen discovery and vaccine design by analyzing large datasets from various sources to identify patterns and predict potential antigens that could be effective in vaccine development. It can predict the immunogenicity and antigenicity of candidate antigens, model the three-dimensional structures of proteins, and perform molecular docking simulations. AI also expedites the screening of a vast number of potential antigens by automating the analysis of experimental data. Furthermore, it revolutionizes the development of personalized vaccines by analyzing individual genetic and immunological profiles, and integrates diverse data types to uncover new insights into the pathogenesis of TB and the immune responses to infection.

The management of TB is pivotal in curbing the spread of this pervasive disease; however, therapeutic advancements in combating TB are impeded by a myriad of developmental challenges. Anti-tuberculosis pharmaceuticals are bifurcated into two distinct tiers. The first-line regimen predominantly comprises isoniazid, rifamycins, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, which are the cornerstone of therapy for non-drug-resistant and drug-sensitive TB cases. In contrast, second-line agents, encompassing levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline (BDQ), and delamanid (DLM), are invariably resorted to in scenarios where drug resistance is established. While new drugs like BDQ and DLM offer hope for treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), issues such as diagnostic failures, lengthy treatment regimens, and adverse side effects pose significant hurdles. Current therapies focus on both drug-sensitive and latent TB infections, but new strategies are essential to enhance treatment efficacy and patient outcomes.

This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of TB vaccine and therapeutic drug development. By examining recent advances and ongoing research, it highlights the potential for novel vaccines and therapeutic strategies to transform TB prevention and treatment, ultimately contributing to global efforts to end the TB epidemic.
Antigen selection for TB vaccines

The selection of antigens is a crucial step in the development of effective TB vaccines. This process involves identifying components that can elicit a strong and protective immune response. The advancement of bioinformatics and AI has significantly enhanced our ability to identify and evaluate potential TB antigens.
Overview of TB antigen categories

With the rapid advancement of genomics and proteomics, research on MTB has entered the post-genomic era. Since the completion of the full genome sequencing of the MTB H37Rv strain by the Sanger Center and the Pasteur Institute in 1998, studies on MTB antigens have deepened, laying an important foundation for the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of TB.

bAntigenicity: The antigenicity of proteins is evaluated using the VaxiJen v2.0 server, with a threshold value set at 0.4. In this study, proteins are categorized into four levels of antigenicity based on their antigenicity scores: scores below 0.4 are classified as Low, scores between 0.4 and 0.6 are Moderate, scores between 0.6 and 0.8 are High, and scores of 0.8 or above are Very High
cImmunogenicity: Scores below 0 are classified as Low, scores between 0 and 1 are Moderate, scores between 1 and 10 are High, and scores of 10 or above are Very High
dHydrophilicity:
+Indicates that the antigen has high hydrophilicity, meaning it has good solubility in aqueous solutions or strong interactions with water molecules
-Indicates that the antigen has low hydrophilicity, meaning it has poor solubility in aqueous solutions or weak interactions with water molecules
eAllergenicity:
+Indicates that the antigen may have allergenic properties, meaning it has the potential to trigger allergic reactions in the immune system
-Indicates that the antigen has no known or discovered allergenic properties, meaning it is unlikely to cause allergic reactions
fToxicity:
+Indicates that the antigen has toxicity, potentially causing harm or having harmful effects on organisms
-Indicates that the antigen has no toxicity, or no toxicity has been discovered yet
NA Not Available or Not Applicable

MTB antigens can be categorized based on their biological characteristics, physicochemical properties, and functions. The main categories of MTB antigens include: (1) Cell wall and capsular antigens: MTB's cell wall and capsule contain glycolipids, lipoproteins, and glycoproteins such as cord factor and lipoarabinomannan. These antigens are key for immune activation and vaccine development. (2) Secreted antigens: MTB secretes proteins like Ag85A/B and ESAT-6, which can modulate the host's immune system. These antigens are strong candidates for subunit vaccines due to their immunogenicity and ease of production. (3) Dormancy phase antigens: During dormancy, MTB relies on antigens regulated by the DosR regulon, such as HspX, for survival. These antigens are promising for vaccines targeting latent TB infection. (4) Resuscitation phase antigens: Resuscitation promotion factors (Rpfs) like RpfB are involved in reactivating dormant MTB and are potential antigens for vaccines addressing LTBI (latent tuberculosis infection). (5) BCG regions of difference (RD) antigens: BCG strains lack 16 RD antigens found in MTB, including ESAT-6, which are crucial for pathogenicity. These antigens are important for developing more effective vaccines. In this review, we have compiled a list of 84 MTB antigens that show potential or have demonstrated promising experimental results in TB vaccine development (Table 1).
Role of bioinformatics and AI in antigen selection

The integration of bioinformatics and AI has revolutionized the process of antigen selection in the development of TB vaccines. These technologies enable the systematic analysis and interpretation of vast amounts of biological data, accelerating the identification of potential antigens with high precision and efficiency.

Bioinformatics is essential for managing and analyzing the genomic and proteomic data of MTB. By using databases and computational tools, researchers can predict antigenic epitopes, understand genetic variations across different strains, and model the structural interactions between antigens and the host immune system. This computational approach allows for the efficient narrowing down of potential antigens for further experimental validation, thereby saving both time and resources. In our previous studies, we have developed several multi-epitope vaccines (MEVs) using bioinformatic tools. For instance, we utilized the IEDB database for screening immunodominant T cell epitopes, the ABCpred server for predicting B cell epitopes, and the ANTIGENpro and VaxiJen v2.0 servers for predicting biological properties. Additionally, we employed Allergen FP v.1.0 and AllerTOP v.2.0 for allergenicity prediction, the Expasy ProtParam server for determining physicochemical parameters, the protein-sol server for assessing solubility, and PSIPRED for evaluating the secondary structure of the multi-epitope vaccine. The integrated use of these tools provides a scientific basis for the design and optimization of TB vaccine candidate antigens.

Furthermore, AI enhances these efforts by applying machine learning algorithms to identify patterns and features associated with effective immune responses. The application of AI technology, particularly AlphaFold 2 and its deep learning capabilities, has revolutionized protein structure prediction by achieving atomic-level accuracy. Several studies have utilized AlphaFold 2 in vaccine design, significantly enhancing both the accuracy and speed of the development process. The introduction of AlphaFold 3 has further advanced predictive accuracy by enabling the prediction of complex structures of virtually all molecule types without requiring structural information input. In the context of vaccine design, understanding the spatial structure of antigens is essential for molecular docking and dynamic simulations. Tools such as PatchDock, AutoDock Vina, GROMACS, and AmberTools are employed to predict how antigens bind to immune receptors and to simulate the dynamic behavior of these complexes.

In the next section, to predict the immunogenicity and antigenicity of the key TB antigens under investigation, we utilized VaxiJen v2.0 and IEDB Immunogenicity server for evaluation. Additionally, the Expasy ProtParam tool was used to assess the aliphatic index and grand average of hydropathicity of the antigens, while AllerTOP v.2.0 and ToxinPred were employed to predict antigen allergenicity and toxicity. We focused particularly on 12 MTB antigens with high candidate potential. High-precision protein structure predictions for these antigens were performed using the AlphaFold server, and their protein interactions were predicted using the STRING database. Furthermore, immune simulation predictions conducted through the C-ImmSim server analyzed the ability of these antigens to induce antibodies and cytokines, providing valuable information for vaccine design and antigen selection.

EsxA and EsxB

PDB https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb1WA8/pdb; (b) Proteins interacting with EsxA and EsxB; (c) Observed coexpression in Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv. In the triangle-matrices above, the intensity of color indicates the level of confidence that two proteins are functionally associated, given the overall expression data in the organism; (d, e) Predicted IgM and IgG antibodies and cytokines production induced by EsxA and EsxB

EsxA (ESAT-6, Rv3875) and EsxB (CFP-10, lhp, mtsA10, Rv3874) are two closely related proteins encoded by the RD-1 region of MTB, playing crucial roles in the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and vaccine development for TB. These two proteins are secreted through the ESAT-6 secretion system 1 (ESX-1), also known as the type VII secretion system (T7S). Notably, the RD-1 region is present in pathogenic M. bovis and MTB but absent in BCG strains. EsxA and EsxB form a stable 1:1 complex (Fig. 1a) and interact with other proteins such as eccD1, eccCb1, espl, fbp, esxH, PPE68, and espC (Fig. 1b, c). This complex plays a significant role in MTB virulence. Alexander S. Pym et al. observed that reintroducing ESAT-6 into BCG resulted in significant changes in colony morphology and enhanced virulence.

Regarding immune responses, both EsxA and EsxB are highly immunogenic, recognized by over 70% of TB patients, making them valuable for TB diagnosis in humans and animals. These proteins not only induce B cell-mediated humoral immunity but also activate T lymphocytes to produce IFN-gamma (Fig. 1d and e). Studies have shown that using a mixture of EsxA and EsxB, and TB7.7 as specific antigens can induce MTB-specific immune responses through whole blood stimulation, producing cytokines and chemokines. Antony M Rapulana et al. further discovered that joint stimulation of whole blood with EsxA and EsxB could use IFN-gamma, IL-2, and IP-10 as potential biomarkers to distinguish between LTBI and healthy individuals.

Moreover, EsxA and EsxB play important roles in MTB virulence, leading to host cell lysis and suppression of macrophage responses. Studies have shown that pretreatment of macrophages with recombinant EsxB protein can reduce the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Notably, EsxB can induce potent cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses, accounting for up to 30% of CD8 + T cells in the lungs of MTB-infected mouse models. This finding provides new hope for developing vaccine strategies aimed at inducing CD8 + T cell responses. Given the widespread application of EsxA and EsxB in immunological research and vaccine design, several vaccines, including AEC/BC02, GamTBvac, H56:IC31, and MVATG18598, have incorporated these two proteins as key antigens.
TB10.4 (esxH, cfp7, Rv0288)

EsxH Protein Interactions and Immunological Responses: Structural and Predictive Analysis. (a) Proteins interacting with EsxH; (b) Solution structure of the EsxA-EsxB Complex, PDB https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb2KG7/pdb; (c) Predicted IgM and IgG antibody response induced by EsxH; (d) Predicted cytokine response induced by EsxH

TB10.4, also known as esxH, cfp7, or Rv0288, is a secretory antigen protein isolated from the serum of cattle infected with Mycobacterium bovis. As a member of the ESAT-6 protein family, TB10.4 interacts with proteins such as esxG, espG3, esxB, esxA, and PPE4 (Fig. 2a), which are crucial for its biological functions. EsxG and EsxH have previously been shown to form a stable 1:1 heterodimeric complex, characterized by a core four-helix bundle decorated at both ends by long, highly flexible N- and C-terminal arms, which contain numerous highly conserved residues (Fig. 2b). Encoded by the Rv0288 gene, TB10.4 is downregulated in the attenuated H37Ra strain and plays a crucial role in inducing CD4 + T cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), which are vital for controlling intracellular pathogens like MTB (Fig. 2c). It also activates B-cells, leading to the production of antibodies that can neutralize pathogens and provide immune protection (Fig. 2d). This highlights its central role in mycobacterial pathogenesis and T cell activation.

With respect to the viral vector vaccine strategy, a study by Mariia Sergeeva and colleagues utilized an attenuated influenza virus vector vaccine Flu/THSP expressing MTB antigens TB10.4 and HspX to immunize mice and guinea pigs via the intranasal route. This approach successfully induced CD4+ and CD8+ T cell immune responses and promoted the production of cytokines such as IFN-gamma, IL-2, and TNF-alpha. These immune responses reduced bacterial load in mouse lungs and spleen and improved lung pathology. Notably, compared to the use of BCG alone, the priming with BCG followed by boosting with Flu/THSP vaccine significantly reduced the bacterial load in the lungs and spleens of guinea pigs and markedly improved the pathological morphology of their lungs.

Furthermore, TB10.4 has shown significant immunogenicity and is strongly recognized by T cells from TB patients and BCG vaccinees. Compared to ESAT-6, TB10.4 is more strongly immunologically recognized in TB patients. Building on the Ag85B-ESAT-6 fusion protein, Jes Dietrich and colleagues replaced ESAT-6 with TB10.4 to evaluate its potential as a TB subunit vaccine. Results showed that the Ag85B-TB10.4 fusion protein was comparable in immunogenicity to the BCG vaccine, and TB10.4 was more strongly recognized than ESAT-6. This suggests that TB10.4 has the potential to be an ideal substitute for ESAT-6, providing a new perspective for TB vaccine development. Currently, TB10.4 has become one of the antigen components in TB vaccines such as TB/FLU-05E and MVATG18598, and its application prospects in vaccine development are promising.
esxV (Rv3619c) and esxW (Rv3620c)

EsxV and EsxW are two immunodominant antigens specific to MTB, composed predominantly of alpha-helices and belonging to the ESAT-6 family (Fig. 3a). These antigens are known to interact with a variety of proteins, including EsxL, EsxO, EsxP, EsxK, EsxA, and EsxB (Fig. 3b, c). These interactions are crucial for their biological functions. esxW can stimulate Th1 immune responses and increase IFN-gamma production in peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMCs) from healthy tuberculin-positive (PPD +) donors. The genes encoding esxV and esxW are both located in the RD-9 of the MTB genome (Fig. 3d). Similar to ESAT-6/CFP10, esxV and esxW can form a 1:1 heterodimer complex through interaction. Research indicates that the choice of adjuvants and delivery systems significantly influences the cytokine responses, including those of Th1, Th2, Th17, and Treg, in mice immunized with MTB antigens. Notably, EsxV is the sole antigen that consistently induces antigen-specific Th1 responses and IFN-gamma secretion across all tested adjuvants and delivery systems. When combined with alum or Mycobacterium smegmatis, EsxV also induces significant levels of antigen-specific IgG antibodies (Fig. 3e, f). EsxW, similarly, induces protective immune responses, promoting IFN-gamma production and T cell activation, which suggests its potential as a component in MTB vaccine development (Fig. 3g, h). Based on these findings, esxV and esxW have been incorporated as components in the ID93 + GLA-SA vaccine, while the ID91 repRNA vaccine has also selected esxV as one of its antigens, further demonstrating their potential in TB vaccine development.
Ag85A (fbpA, mpt44, Rv3804c)

Ag85 complex, also known as Fibronectin-binding proteins (Fbps), is a 30-32 kDa family consisting of three proteins: Ag85A, Ag85B, and Ag85C. These proteins are located in the MTB cell wall, have secretory capabilities, and possess important enzymatic mycobacterial acyltransferase activity. As one of the most abundantly secreted proteins by MTB, the Ag85 complex can elicit strong humoral and cellular immune responses, making it a promising candidate antigen for TB vaccine development. Ag85A, a diacylglycerol acyltransferase involved in lipid body formation (Figure S1a), interacts with various proteins such as fbpC, fbpB, lipY, dagK, and esxA (Figure S1b), demonstrating potential to induce Th1-type cytokines. It promotes the production of cytokines including IFN-gamma, TGF-beta, IL-10, and IL-12 (Figure S1c), while also activating B cells to produce Ag85A-specific antibodies (Figure S1d), exhibiting good immunogenicity. Ag85A and Ag85B extracted from BCG and MTB culture filtrates have successfully induced strong T cell proliferation and IFN-gamma production in most LTBI patients, BCG-vaccinated mice, and humans. However, similar effects were not observed in TB patients. In a study by Marta Romano et al., mice initially immunized with an Ag85A-encoding DNA plasmid followed by BCG boost showed significantly improved survival rates and enhanced CD4+ and CD8+ T cell-mediated IFN-gamma responses. Conversely, a regimen involving initial BCG immunization followed by an Ag85A-encoding DNA plasmid boost promoted IFN-gamma secretion and IL-17 production but did not improve mouse survival rates. Based on these findings, Ag85A has been selected as a primary candidate antigen for MTB vaccine development. Several vaccines, including GamTBvac, Ad5Ag85A, TB/FLU-01L, TB/FLU-04L, ChAdOx1.85A, and MVA85A, have incorporated Ag85A into their antigen components.
Ag85B (fbpB, mpt59, Rv1886c)

Ag85B, a key secretory protein of MTB, plays multiple biological roles. It not only participates in cell wall mycolyltransferase activity, promoting cell wall synthesis (Figure S1e), but is also considered an important target due to its potential in immune protection and drug development. Ag85B interacts with proteins such as fbpC, Rv1885c, fbpA, esxA, and mpt64 (Figure S1f), inducing B cell-mediated humoral immune responses (Figure S1g) and eliciting T cell responses in humans and mice, particularly enhancing the production of the Th1-type cytokine IFN-gamma (Figure S1h). In animal model studies, an immunization strategy combining the mincle agonist UM-1098 and ESAT6/Ag85B successfully induced protective Th1 and Th17 immune responses, significantly increasing the secretion levels of IFN-gamma, IL-17A, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), IL-5, and other cytokines, as well as antigen-specific IgG, IgG2c, and IgG1 antibodies, while reducing bacterial load in mouse lungs. A. Weinrich Olsen and colleagues developed a TB subunit vaccine based on the Ag85B and ESAT-6 fusion protein, which induced effective long-term memory immunity in mice, providing protection levels comparable to the BCG vaccine and demonstrating high efficacy against TB. Research by Marcus A. Horwitz et al. also confirmed that rBCG30 expressing Ag85B, used as a booster for the BCG vaccine, significantly enhanced BCG's protective efficacy. Given Ag85B's significant role in eliciting immune responses, it has become a popular candidate antigen in vaccine development. Currently, several vaccines, including AEC/BC02, H56:IC31, MVATG18598, rBCG30, and ID91 repRNA, incorporate Ag85B as a component.
PPE18 (mtb39a, Rv1196)

PPE18, also known as MTB39a or Rv1196, is a cell wall-associated protein encoded by the Rv1196 gene (Figure S2a). As a member of the PE/PPE protein family, PPE18 interacts with various proteins such as esxK, esxL, PE13, esxW, and esxV (Figure S2b). This family accounts for a significant proportion (8-10%) of the MTB genome and is characterized by the Pro-Pro-Glu (PPE) repeat sequence in the N-terminal region. PPE family proteins have the ability to regulate cytokine secretion and influence host cell apoptosis and necrosis. PPE18 exhibits significant immunogenicity (Figure S2c and d) and can bind to Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) on the surface of macrophages. Through activation of the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, it promotes the production of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, thereby promoting a Th2-type immune response. Simultaneously, PPE18 suppresses the Th1-type immune response by specifically downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12 and TNF-alpha. Additionally, PPE18 can inhibit antigen presentation by MHC class II molecules, impair CD4+ T cell activation, and suppress B cell activation and antibody production. These characteristics reveal PPE18's crucial role in MTB immune evasion.

The virulence factor properties of PPE18 have also been confirmed in mouse models. Infection with MTB strains lacking PPE18 resulted in reduced bacterial load, less organ damage, and increased survival rates in mice. Furthermore, a DNA vaccine encoding PPE18 showed protective effects in mice, although not as effective as the BCG vaccine, but significantly reduced lung bacterial burden compared to the control group. These findings support further research into PPE18 as a vaccine candidate component. Currently, some vaccines such as M72/AS01E have incorporated PPE18 into their antigen combinations.
Rv1813c

Rv1813c is a latency antigen discovered in MTB (Figure S2e), co-regulated by regulatory factors MprA and DosR. As a conserved hypothetical protein, Rv1813c interacts with various proteins such as Rv2030c, acg, Rv3127, Rv1733c, and fdxA (Figure S2f), which are crucial for its functions. A key function of Rv1813c is its ability to target host cell mitochondria and manipulate host metabolic pathways. When expressed in eukaryotic cells, Rv1813c localizes to the mitochondrial intermembrane space and increases ATP production in host cells by promoting the oxidative phosphorylation pathway. This metabolic adjustment is beneficial for MTB as it helps avoid the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cell apoptosis. Moreover, cells expressing Rv1813c show delayed release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, which is part of the early defense mechanism of macrophages infected with MTB. Thus, Rv1813c influences both the metabolic and apoptotic responses of host cells.

Rv1813c also demonstrates strong immunogenicity (Figure S2g and h) and can be recognized by over 70% of TB patients. In mouse models, Rv1813c can induce strong CD4+ T cell responses, achieved through the expression of IFN-gamma/TNF and TNF/IL-2 cytokines. Compared to other candidate antigens such as Rv3620, Rv3619, Rv2608, and Rv3478, Rv1813c induces the highest number of CD8 + T cells expressing IFN-gamma and/or TNF. Furthermore, Rv1813c can provide protective effects in MTB-infected mice by generating antigen-specific IgG2c antibodies to reduce bacterial load in the lungs. Given these characteristics of Rv1813c, it has been incorporated into subunit vaccines ID93 + GLA-SE and MVATG18598 as a potential vaccine component, aiming to enhance protection against TB.
pepA (mtb32a, Rv0125)
