passages.text: Vestibulo-oculomotor examination characteristics

In the 22 patients who performed vestibulo-oculomotor examinations, 9 (40.9%) were abnormal (Table 2). Bilateral impairments were revealed in 6 of them, and unilateral impairments in 3, involving one or more SCs (Figure 4a-d). Seven of them were complicated by symptomatic or subclinical hearing loss (ipsilateral or contralateral to the damaged SCs), or tinnitus (Figure 4e).

Vestibulo-oculomotor examinations and hearing loss in FD patients. A. Caloric test in P19, showing decreased SPV bilaterally (LC+LW = 2.5 /s, RC+RW = 3.3 /s), indicating bilateral weakness of horizontal semicircular canals; B. vHIT in P19, showing reduced gain in 3 semicircular canals bilaterally (LA, LP and RA), inconsistent with the distribution of a single nerve or vessel; C. Pure tone audiometry in P19, showing impaired threshold on the high frequency of the left side (35 dB HL on 4 kHz, 45 dB HL on 8 kHz). D. Dysfunction of semicircular canals in all the patients identified by caloric test and vHIT. E. Comorbidity of vestibular impairment and hearing loss in the patients.

The disease duration in the patient group (Table 2 and Figure 5a-d) with impaired vestibulo-oculomotor performance was significantly longer than that in the patients with normal vestibulo-oculomotor function (32.0 +- 12.4 VS 17.9 +- 14.6, p = 0.036). The MSSI (p = 0.024) and SVDS (p = 0.028) in the vestibulo-oculomotor deficiency group were significantly higher than normal. The incidence rate of vestibulo-oculomotor deficiency in patients with symptomatic hearing loss was significantly higher than that in patients with normal hearing (p = 0.040). The other clinical subgroups showed no significant differences in the rates of vestibulo-oculomotor deficiency.
Clinical characteristics of the patients with/without visuo-oculomotor or vestibulo-oculomotor deficiencies. (*: p < 0.05; **: p < 0.01).

Besides the 9 patients with defective vestibulo-oculomotor performance, 1 patient who did not undergo vestibulo-oculomotor tests rotated to one side of his body by an angle > 45  in Fukuda stepping test during clinical examination. Thus, the total number of patients with peripheral vestibular dysfunction was 10. The plasma Lyso-Gb3 in the peripheral vestibular dysfunction group were significantly higher than normal [80.79(40.00,97.80) VS 7.95(5.06,64.04), p = 0.035] (Figure 5e).
Discussion

There is a high incidence of auditory symptoms and not rare incidence of vestibular symptoms in our FD cohort, coincident with the previously studies reporting an incidence between 19 and 87%. Tinnitus may be the first auditory symptom, affecting approximately 27 ~ 38% of adult patients. Vestibular symptoms or subclinical vestibular deficits were identified in 25 ~ 80% of FD patients. Weak response in the caloric tests, indicating the peripheral vestibular deficits, was observed in the patients with severe systematic symptoms. It is speculated that the mechanism of hearing impairment in FD patients is likely the damage to the cochlea itself, caused by Gb3 deposition in the stria vascularis and spiral ligament of the cochlea, rather than damage to the internal auditory artery (IAA) or auditory nerve. Our data showed that the prevalence of peripheral vestibular dysfunction in patients with symptomatic hearing loss was significantly higher than that in patients with normal hearing, suggesting that the damage of vestibular organs often accompanies the damage of the cochlea, thus they may have a common pathological mechanism, which might be the degeneration caused by the deposition of Gb3 in the stria vascularis.

annotations.text: damage to the internal auditory artery

passages.text: The characteristics of peripheral vestibular dysfunction in our study also support the above mechanism. Nearly half of the patients who underwent vHIT or caloric testing showed abnormalities suggesting peripheral vestibular dysfunction. It is important to note that peripheral vestibular damage in these patients is not consistent with the distribution area of vestibular nerve (VN) branches. The VN is divided into the superior and inferior vestibular nerves, the former innervating the anterior and horizontal SCs, and the latter the posterior SCs. In our patients, reduced vestibulo-ocular reflex gain or compensatory saccades in a single SC, or in SCs on different sides, were frequently present and could not be explained by dysfunction of the superior or inferior vestibular nerves. A few literatures have studied the vestibular function of FD patients. For example, Carmona et al. reported that 70% of vestibular and hearing impairment in FD patients could not be explained by lesions of a single blood vessel or nerve. Consistent with this finding, our study also suggests that the peripheral vestibular dysfunction in Fabry patients is probably due to the lesions of the vestibular organ itself, rather than the damage of the IAA or VN.

In contrast to the vestibulo-oculomotor deficiency, the visuo-oculomotor deficiency in FD patients, which suggests the central vestibular dysfunction, was reported less frequently. Our patients had widespread visuo-oculomotor deficiency. Their deficits in saccades, SPM, and OKN were more common than in normal controls, indicating widespread impairment of the structures involving those eye movements. Those structures are mainly located in the brain stem and cerebellum (Figure 6). This feature is similar to CSVD and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease, but different from most focal cerebral infarctions, which usually result in apparent gaze palsy with abnormalities in only a few visuo-oculomotor items. The incidence rates of spontaneous nystagmus, GEN, and saccadic intrusions in our patients were similar to that in normal controls, indicating that there might be no significant damage to the gaze stabilizing system. This also differs from focal infratentorial infarctions, in which marked spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus is common.

infons.name: Diffuse Lewy Body Disease with Gaze Palsy

passages.text: Schema of the brain structures related with visuo-oculomotor control (left row) and the manifestations of damage to them (right row). (PIVC, parieto-insular vestibular cortex; PIC, posterior insular cortex; FEF, frontal eye fields; DLPFC, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; PEF, parietal eye fields; basal ganglia, BG; GEN, gaze-evoked nystagmus; SC, superior colliculus; INC, the interstitial nucleus of cajal; PPRF, paramedian pontine reticular formation; DRN, dorsal raphe nucleus; VN, the vestibular nuclei; NPH, the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi.).

FD is often prone to affect the posterior circulation system, which may lead to ischemic dysfunction of its territory, mainly involving the brain stem and cerebellum. However, according to our data, the patients with infratentorial lesions on MR do not seem to manifest central vestibular dysfunction more commonly. The similarities of their visuo-oculomotor abnormalities with CSVD and degenerative diseases suggest that other complex mechanisms might be involved besides infratentorial ischemic damage. On one hand, the patients might have small vessel lesions at some structures in the cerebral hemispheres (Figure 6), which also play a role in the visuo-oculomotor control. On the other hand, autopsy and mouse models have confirmed the deposition of Lyso-Gb3 in the neurons of FD, causing visuo-oculomotor abnormalities similar to those seen in some neurodegenerative diseases.

Certain visuo-oculomotor deficiencies appear to be related to the severity of the patients' condition. For example, saccade abnormalities, especially slow saccades, are more likely to be seen in male patients, and these patients, together with the patients with hypermetria, have lower alpha-Gal A activity and higher plasma Lyso-Gb3 levels. Patients with prolonged saccade latencies have longer disease duration and higher MSSI. Patients with defective SPM also have lower alpha-Gal A activity. Although the rates of visuo-oculomotor deficiencies in the patients with/without MR lesions appear to be similar, the higher SVDS scores in those with prolonged saccade latency, hypometria, saccadic pursuits, and defective OKN might indicate a greater overall burden of CSVD. Similar damage of central vestibular system was also reported in Gaucher's disease as biomarkers to monitor neurological deterioration. Therefore, the presence of extensive visuo-oculomotor abnormalities can also be used as a biomarker to predict or monitor the progression of FD.

Peripheral vestibular damage may also be a biomarker of FD progression according to the current study. Our data showed that patients with impaired peripheral vestibular function had longer disease duration, higher MSSI, and higher plasma Lyso-Gb3 levels, indicating a more severe overall disease burden. Interestingly, the SVDS in those patients were also higher, suggesting that peripheral vestibular damage and central small vessel disease seem to parallel. This corroborates the above speculation that the mechanism of peripheral vestibular damage in FD may be the deposition of substrates in the stria vascularis of the inner ear, similar to and simultaneous with the deposition in the endothelium of small vessels in the brain.

Although the above evidence supports the pathology of Gb3 deposition, the pathogenic pathway remains unclear. It is definitely known that the deposition of Gb3 in FD patients is followed by inflammatory activation. The binding of Gb3 to toll-like receptor 4 can trigger Notch1 signaling and activate the nuclear factor kappa B signaling cascade, which results in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to a chronic inflammatory state and associated vasculopathy. The long-lasting inflammation results in fibrosis and tissue injury. As a small anatomical structure, the inner ear could be vulnerable to inflammation. Recently we have identified a spectrum of inflammatory cytokines (ICs) which are upregulated in FD patients and positively correlate with disease burden, especially IL-8, which is higher in the high MSSI subgroup than in the low MSSI subgroup. It can be speculated that the vestibular dysfunctions, which also showed some relevance with MSSI in this study, might be accompanied by the upregulation of those ICs and result from an inflammatory pathway.

Since both central and peripheral vestibular damage seem to parallel the progression of the disease in our study, VNG and peripheral vestibular examination could be used as a method of surveillance in FD. When vestibular dysfunction is identified, especially with the pattern of: (1) a wide-spread visuo-oculomotor deficits, and (2) peripheral vestibular organ damage inconsistent with the distribution of a single VN branch or IAA, a multi-system evaluation should be conducted to early discover the damage of important organs such as heart and kidney.

Because of the limitations of sample size and non-normal distributions of part of the data in our study, some significant associations might have been missed. For example, FD can cause extensive brainstem and cerebellar dysfunction, which theoretically leads to gaze stabilizing system impairment and visual fixation disorder. However, although the incidence rate of saccadic intrusions in the patient group seemed to be higher than that in the control group, the difference was not statistically significant, which might be due to the small sample size, or might be because the characteristics of saccade intrusions in the patients are different from the normal population despite the same incidence rate, such as the frequency, duration, amplitude, and saccadic interval, which needs more detailed investigation. A multi-center study with a larger sample size and a follow-up study to get normally distributed data are needed. Besides, more research should be done to explore the correlations between the upregulated ICs and the vestibular dysfunctions to reveal the role of inflammation in the pathogenesis.
Conclusion

This study shows that patients with FD in China may have extensive central and peripheral vestibular dysfunctions, with the deposition of substrates in vestibular organs being a likely mechanism. Therefore, the vestibular function may reflect the burden of systemic substrates deposition and serve as a candidate clinical marker to monitor disease progression in FD.

passages.text: Loss of flavonoids homeostasis leads to pistillody in sua-CMS of Nicotiana tabacum

The homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures (pistillody) causes cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS). This phenomenon is widely present in plants, and might be induced by intracellular communication (mitochondrial retrograde signaling), but its systemic regulating mechanism is still unclear. In this study, morphological observation showed that the stamens transformed into pistil-like structures, leading to flat and dehiscent pistils, and fruit set decrease in sua-CMS (MS K326, somatic fusion between Nicotiana. tabacum L. K326 and Nicotiana suaveolens). Transcriptome data analysis presented that the expression levels of B-class MADS genes, including pMADS1, GLO1, GLO2, pMADS2.1, pMADS2.2, significantly reduced in the pistil-like structure of sua-CMS. DEGs were enriched in flavonoid and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathways. Transcriptome and metabolomics analysis revealed that the expression levels of CHI/CHS (key enzymes regulating flavonoid synthesis), and the contents of flavonoids reduced significantly in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS. Chemical fluorescence staining assay showed that reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were higher in the pistil-like structure of sua-CMS. Application of external flavonoids (hesperetin) reduced the frequency of pistillody and ROS levels. These results suggested that the metabolism of flavonoids played important roles in regulating pistillody through ROS in sua-CMS. Our study provides new insights into the regulatory mechanism of pistillody in plants.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12870-025-06122-8.
Introduction

Male sterile lines are crucial breeding tools for harnessing hybrid vigor or heterosis in hybrid crops, and they also provide valuable materials for studying stamen and pollen development as well as nuclear-cytoplasmic interactions. Male-sterile lines include cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS) or nuclear-controlled environment-sensitive genic male sterility (EGMS). CMS is a maternally inherited phenomenon preventing the production of functional pollen by virtue of mitochondrial dysfunction, and has great value in theoretical research and breeding application. Some CMS species exhibit a novel phenotype that transforms all or parts of the stamen into pistils or pistil-like structures, this phenomenon refers to pistillody. Pistillody causes the pistil dysfunction, reduces pollination efficiency and seed yield, and may also hinder the fertility restoration of CMS lines. The research on the genetic regulation mechanism of pistillody has extremely important theoretical and practical significance for plant seed breeding and production.

Pistillody is widely present in the plant kingdom, and firstly reported in the genera Papaver and Salix, and subsequently reported in Hypericum nudiflorum, pepper, rice, wheat, Alternanthera philoxeroides, Brassica campestris, cabbage, Aegilops, etc. [ 4-7]. Similar to the genetic regulation mechanism of CMS, pistillody is controlled by nuclear-cytoplasm interaction. This interaction between nuclear and cytoplasm occurs through an intracellular signaling pathway termed mitochondrial retrograde signaling (MRS). Moreover, rapamycin (TOR) signaling also linked to MRS. In eukaryotes, such as yeast, mammalian, positive/negative regulatory factors and mitochondrial Ca2+ are involved in MRS. Interestingly, none of the regulatory genes involved in yeast or animal MRS seem to be conserved in plants, indicating that MRS has evolved in different directions across kingdoms. Major MRS components identified in plants so far include ANAC017-related, ABI4 and WRKY, as well as the cyclin-dependent kinase CDKE.

In higher plants, the determination of floral organ identity is explained by the ABCDE model. The alterations in the expression patterns of nuclear class B MADS-box induce the pistillody. Mitochondrial genes, such as orf25, orf260cra, regulate the expression of nuclear class-B MADS-box genes through MRS, and cause pistillody. Although, we have known that the mitochondrial genes-MRS-class B MADS-box regulates the occurrence of pistillody, the transcript and metabolism landscape is still unclear, more factors remain to be identified.

The rapid improvement of high-throughput sequencing and computer analysis technology enables the production of various omics data. Various tools and analysis methods based on the analysis of omics data, including protein-protein interaction network analysis (PPI), weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), neural network analysis, etc., are developed. The molecular mechanism of CMS or pistillody, have been elucidated by omics data analysis. For example, WGCNA analysis explored the relationships between modules and pistillody, and co-expression network and GO analysis identified genes associated with pistillody. Comparative complete mitochondrial genome and transcriptome sequencing explored the potential genetic mechanism of the CMS in Nicotiana tabacum. In sum, omics data analysis shows the great advantages in the study of system biology and species with complex genetic background.

The sua-CMS (MS K326) were obtained through the somatic cell fusion between the nucleus of N. tabacum L. "K326" (K326) and the cytoplasm of Nicotiana suaveolens, while the gla-CMS were through the cytoplasm of Nicotiana glauca and the nucleus of K326. sua-CMS lines show homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures (pistillody) and are therefore male sterile, and gla-CMS have dehiscent stamens but not pistillody. Sua-CMS is the only sterile cytoplasm with economic value as having no negative effects on agronomic or quality traits in tobacco, and is the most widely used sterile system in production. The complete mitochondrial genome of sua-CMS (HD) is sequenced using the PacBio and Illumina Hiseq technology, and sua-CMS (HD)-specific mitochondrial genes have been identified by BLAST analysis, but the systematic molecular mechanism associated with the development of sua-CMS have never been reported. In the present study, in order to identify the metabolic processes and transcription factors that might contribute to pistillody in sua-CMS, RNA-Seq and un-targeted metabolome detection were conducted using the stamens, pistil and pistil-like structures from K326 (male fertility), sua-CMS (MS K326, pistillody) and gla-CMS (male sterile) lines. Transcriptomic and metabolomic data analysis constructed a comprehensive landscape of the genetic network and gene expression patterns associated with pistillody in sua-CMS, and identified the functional genes and metabolites. The results indicated that the expression levels of class B MADS decreased, and the levels of flavonoids reduced, while reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulated in the stamen and pistil-like structures of sua-CMS. Application of flavonoids reduced the pistillody ratio and ROS levels of sua-CMS (MS K326). Our research provides important insights into the molecular mechanism underlying pistillody widely present in plants.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and growth conditions

The cytoplasmic male sterile line sua-K326 and gla-CMS were obtained through the somatic cell fusion between the nucleus of N. tabacum L. "K326" and the cytoplasm of Nicotiana suaveolens and Nicotiana glauca, respectively. sua-CMS lines showed homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures (pistillody), while gla-CMS had dehiscent stamens. Seedlings of N. tabacum(MS K326, sua-CMS; gla-CMS, Gla K326; K326)were grown in an Light incubator (BINDER, German) with a temperature of 25 +- 1 C, a light intensity of 800 micromol m- 2 s- 1, a light stage of 16 h/8 h(day/night), and a relative humidity of 70 +- 1%. Seedlings of uniform size were selected and transplanted to the soil pot (Matrix ratio of turf: vermiculite: perlite = 1:1:1), when it had four leaves in the greenhouse of the College of Ecology and Environment, Yunnan University, located in Kunming, Yunnan, China (N:24 49'54'' E:102 51'6''). The plants were manually watered weekly and fertilized monthly with water-soluble fertilizers (N: P: K, 20:20:20 and 0.5% trace elements) (Sichuan Demei).
Fruits set, fruit and seed weight analysis

Styles of sua-CMS (MS K326) were classified into normal cylindrical, flattened, and split dehiscent ones according to the morphological characteristics. Flowers in ten plants of sua-CMS (MS K326) were pollinated, and fruits set ratio, fruits and seed weight were compared among normal cylindrical, flattened, and split dehiscent styles at 30 d after pollination.
Samples for metabolomics and transcriptomics analysis

Flower buds at stage S1 and S3 were collected. The pistil and stamen were collected separately at stage 3. Pistil and stamen at stage 1 were pooled sampling, as they were too small to be separated. Three biological replicates were set up for each subgroup. The flowers were quickly placed in liquid nitrogen and then stored at -80  C for metabolomics and transcriptomics analysis.
Metabolomics and data analysis

The stamens/pistils were ground into powder by liquid nitrogen, and resuspended with 1 mL of 80% methanol. After extraction on ice, the sample was centrifuged in a freezing centrifuge for 15 min (12000 rpm, 4  C). The supernatant was retained for subsequent liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis. Metabolomics analyses were performed as previously reported. Principal component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) were performed using the MetaboAnalyst R package. The log2-corrected data were screened for metabolites with Fold Change >= 2, and p-value < 0.05 for Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses.
Transcriptomics and data analysis

Total RNA from different samples was extracted using RNAprep Pure Plant kit (DP441, Tiangen, China), and RNA accuracy was evaluated using Biometra gel electrophoresis. The cDNA libraries were constructed according to the previous methods and sequenced on Illumina 2000 sequencing platform. The reference genome was N. tabacum K326 (https://solgenomics.sgn.cornell.edu/organism/Nicotiana_tabacum/genome). HISAT2 was used for gene annotation, PCA and differential gene expression were analyzed with FactoMineR and DESeq2 R packages. Cluster Profiler R packages were used for Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis.
WGCNA analysis

The WGCNA R package was applied to construct the co-expression network. A soft threshold was set to make the genes in the network confirm to the scale-free topology distribution. The setting methods and principles were performed as previously described. The co-expression networks were visualized using cystoscope.
In situ hybridization of pMASD1 in flower buds

To investigate the in-situ expression pattern of pMADS1 gene in N. tabacum (MS K326, Gla K326 and K326), we performed RNA in situ hybridization analysis in flower buds at S1 stage, as previous reports. Tissue sections after in situ hybridization were analyzed in the Histo-Line Laboratories S700 and photographed on Leica THUNDER Imager Tissue.
External application of flavonoids on flower bud of sua-CMS

The sua-CMS with flower buds at stage 1 was sprayed with flavonoids on leaf and bud. The concentration of flavonoids was as the following, 50mM of quercetin, kaempferol and naringin, and 25 mM of hesperidin. H2O was sprayed as the control, three replicates for each treatment. A total of 15 plants were treated. It was sprayed every 3 days. After 30 days, the pistillody ratio in each repeat was calculated.
CM-H2DCFDA staining of ROS

To visualize the ROS levels in vivo, the flower buds of K326, sua-CMS and gla-CMS at stage S0 were cut into 10-micrometer sections using a cryostat microtome (Leica CM1950). Then the slides were stained with 5 microM of 2', 7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (CM-H2DCFDA) (Sigma-Aldrich) as previously described. In control, CM-H2DCFDA was replaced by DMSO. The ROS levels in flower bud were quantified by measuring fluorescence pixel intensity using Image-Pro Plus software (Media Cybernetics). Three biological replicates were performed.
Statistical analysis

Homoscedasticity of variances were tested in SPSS, and then the data were analyzed using the statistical software GraphPad Prism 7. Student's t-test or ANOVA (analysis of variance) was performed to detect statistical differences.
Results
Pistillody occurred frequently in alloplasmic line of sua-CMS

sua-CMS and gla-CMS shared the same nucleus background of K326, while were with different cytoplasm (Fig. 1a). sua-CMS showed homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures named pistillody. Pistillody was not only due to male sterile, but also caused the occurrence of pistil abnormality, including the flat and dehiscent pistil (Fig. 1b). The flat pistil occurred with the frequency of 62.30%, and dehiscent pistil with the frequency of 17.29% (Table 1). Compared with that in cylindrical style of sua-CMS, fruit set of the flat and dehiscent styles significantly decreased after pollination. The fruit set rate is the lowest in the dehiscent styles (Table 1) (Fig. 1c). Furthermore, the fruit and seed weight also decreased when the flat and dehiscent styles were pollinated (Table 1). These results showed that the pistillody caused abnormal development of both stamens and pistils, and further reduced fruits set ratio and seed yield.

The contents of flavonoids and phenolic acids significantly reduced in sua-CMS lines

To investigate the metabolic mechanism of pistillody in sua-CMS, the flower bud of K326 (male fertility), gla-CMS (male sterile) and sua-CMS (pistillody) at S1 and S3 development stages were collected (Fig. 1d). We detected the differential metabolites in the stamen, degenerate stamen, pistil or pistil-like structures by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry technology. Metabolomics analysis showed that there were significant inter-group differences among samples, and principal component PC1 and PC2 accounted for 32.7% and 19.8% of the total sample variance, respectively (Fig. 2a). The metabolites in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS at stage 1 were most similar to that in pistil of K326 at stage 3 (Fig. 2a), revealing that pistillody of sua-CMS happened not only at the morphological appearance, but also at the metabolite level. Notably, flavonoids and phenolic acids accounted for the most abundant differential metabolites of three groups at different stages (Fig. 2b and c). In addition, lipids, amino acids and alkaloids also accounted for a larger proportion among differential metabolites (Fig. 2b and c).

Comparative analysis finds that there are 18 metabolites both detected in K_vs_MS, G_vs_M, KS_vs_MS, GS_vs_MS (Fig. 2d). Among these 18 differential metabolites, phenolic compounds, flavonoids including kaempherol derivative (pmp001311, Zmhp102730, Lmmp003817) and quercetin derivative (Zmcp002666) accounted for the largest proportion (Fig. 2e). The differential metabolites mentioned above may be involved in regulating pistillody development from stage S1 to S3.

The expression levels of B-class MADSsignificantly reduced, and DEGs are enriched in flavonoid and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathways insua-CMS

To explore the potential regulatory genes involved in pistillody of sua-CMS, the DEGs of the stamen (or pistil-like structures) and pistil of K326, sua-CMS and gla-CMS at S1 and S2 development stages were detected using high-throughput RNA transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) technology. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that PC1 and PC2 accounted for 23.8% and 14.5% of the total sample variance, respectively (Fig. 3a). The principal components of pistil and pistil-like structures of sua-CMS (M) at stage 1 overlapped with that in pistil of K326 (KP) at stage 3 (Fig. 3a), indicating that the gene expression pattern in pistil and pistil-like structures of sua-CMS at stage 1 was more inclined to that in the pistil of K326. This revealed that pistillody of sua-CMS also occurred at the genetical level.

At stage 1, there were 5304 differential genes between K326 and sua-CMS, in which 1397 genes were up-regulated, 3907 genes were down-regulated. Between the pistil/stamen of gla-CMS and sua-CMS at stage 1, 1805 differential genes were detected, and among them 765 genes were up-regulated, 1040genes were down-regulated (Fig. 3b). At S3 stage, 15,382 differential genes were found between the stamen of K326 and pistil-like structures of sua-CMS, 8207genes with high expression and 7175 genes with low expression. 8241 differential genes were detected between gla-CMS and sua-CMS stamen, 4685 genes were up-expressed, 3556 genes were down-expressed (Fig. 3b). Whether in the S1 or S3 stage, the number of differential genes between gla-CMS and sua-CMS was fewer than that between K326_vs_sua-CMS. This may be due to the significant phenotypic differences between MS K326 (sterile) and K326 (fertile), while MS K326 and Gla.S K326 were both male sterile.

Analysis of differential transcription factors among four groups revealed that the number of ARR-B involved in signal transduction was the highest, following by the AP2-EREBP and NAC family. Notably, 225 MADS transcription factors responsible for homologous transformation of floral organs were also differentially expressed (Fig. 3c). B-class MADS, NAC, MYB26 and bHLH transcription factors showed the highest differential expression levels among different samples (Fig. 3d). It was worth noting that the expression levels of 5 B-class MADS genes (pMADS1, GLO1, GLO2, pMADS2.1, pMADS2.2) decreased in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS (Fig. 3d). This down-expression might be responsible for the pistillody of sua-CMS.

There were 588 common DEGs in four groups, and these DEGs were mainly enriched in GO terms related to trans-membrane signal transport and redox reactions, such as channel activity, oxidoreductase activity (Fig. 3e and f). This pathway genes might be related to the MRS pathway associated with pistillody. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis showed that the genes were enriched in flavonoid and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathways in four groups (Fig. 3g). The products of these metabolic pathways may have a significant impact on pistillody.

WGCNA and correlation analysis identified flavonoids and B-classMADSgenes to be key regulator in pistillody ofsua-CMS

We further performed WGCNA, co-expression network and correlation analysis to identify the key regulators of pistillody in sua-CMS. Among 11 modules (Fig. 4a), the MM.yellow module had the greatest positive correlation with pistillody of sua-CMS, while the MM.turquoise module showed the highest negative correlation (Fig. 4a and b). The modules MM.yellow and MM.turquoise contained 7902 DEGs (Supplementary Table 1), including five B-class MADS genes (pMADS1, GLO1, GLO2, pMADS2.1, pMADS2.2). These genes had high connectivity within the module, indicating their central role in regulating pistillody (Fig. 4c). Correlation analysis between DEGs and differential metabolites identified 15 flavonoids (Fig. 4d). These flavonoids were highly related to the flavonoid and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis genes (R value > 0.8) (Fig. 5d). At stage 3, MWS1179 (Naringen-7-O-glucoside) and MWSHY0137 (Naringen (5,7,4 '- Trihydroxyflavanone) decreased by 7.47 folds and 2.07 folds in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS, respectively, compared to that in the stamen of K326. While MWS1003 (Laricitrin) increased most significantly by 5.12-folds (Supplementary Table 2). Flavonoid and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathway analysis showed that the expression levels of CHI, CHS reduced significantly in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS (Fig. 4e). Both of them were key enzyme genes regulating flavonoid synthesis (Fig. 4f). The above results showed that down expression of flavonoid biosynthesis pathway genes and reduction of flavonoid contents might be responsible for the pistillody of sua-CMS.

pmads1transcripts decreased at the stamen and carpel primordium ofsua-CMS detected by in situ hybridization

To further confirm that the transcripts of pmads1 did decrease at the stage when stamens and carpels differentiated, we performed RNA in situ hybridization in flower bud of sua-CMS, gla-CMS and K326. The results showed that the stamen primordium developed in K326 and gla-CMS of stage 1, while hardly detected at sua-CMS, indicating that pistillody were occurring at this stage. RNA in situ hybridization revealed the expression levels of pmads1 were higher in the stamen and carpel primordium of K326, while was the lowest in that of sua-CMS (Fig. 5). These lower expression levels of pmads1 at the stamens and carpels primordium might be related to the pistillody of sua-CMS.

Flavonoids did regulate the pistillody ofsua-CMS

To verify the effect of flavonoid reduction on pistillody of sua-CMS, exogenous flavonoids, including quercetin, kaempferol, naringin and hesperidin, were sprayed on the flower bud before stage 1 of sua-CMS. The results showed that the proportion of pistillody decreased significantly after spraying exogenous flavonoids compared to that in control. Among them, naringin and hesperidin were most effective, and reduced the ratio of pistillody by 15.9% and 20.7%, respectively (Fig. 6), suggesting that the flavonoids did regulate the pistillody of sua-CMS.

Flavonoids affect the pistillody ofsua-CMSby regulating ROS contents

The ROS signal pathway play a crucial role in plant reproduction, while flavonols modulate the ROS homeostasis through the nonenzymatic antioxidant mechanism, and we then ask whether the reduction of flavonols in the pistil-like structure of sua-CMS affects stamen development through modulating ROS homeostasis. To test this possibility, the ROS levels in flower buds at stage 1 were compared by CM-H2DCFDA staining. The result revealed that the fluorescence intensity in the stamen and pistil primordium of sua-CMS was the highest, following by that in gla-CMS (Fig. 7a). The ROS levels in flower bud of K326 was the lowest (Fig. 7b), indicating that ROS was a potential regulator in pistillody. Furthermore, we treated the flower bud at stage S0 of sua-CMS with hesperetin, and water was also sprayed as the control. CM-H2DCFDA staining showed that the fluorescence intensity in the stamen and pistil primordium of sua-CMS treated with flavonoids was significantly lower than that in the control, indicating that the flavonols did affect the ROS level. Therefore, the decrease of flavonoids might lead to the ROS accumulation, and then affect pistillody of sua-CMS.

Discussion
Pistillody occurred frequently insua-CMS

In plants, the male sterility system has traditionally been used for hybrid breeding. In tobacco (N. tabacum), over 30 male sterile lines have been developed, all of which were derived from somatic protoplast fusion or the traditional breeding. Among them, sua-CMS is the only sterile cytoplasm thus far identified without negative effects on growth or quality, and is widely used in heterosis breeding and to produce hybrids. The pistil phenotype of sua-CMS is similar to that of the maintainer lines except male sterility, and can normally obtain offspring through pollination. In this study, sua-CMS (MS K326) showed homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures and were therefore male sterile, and pistils also developed abnormally, with flat and dehiscent styles. Fruit set, fruits and seed weight significantly decreased after pollinating with the maintainer line. This led to severe losses in seed production. The difference in cytoplasm origin may be the reason for the phenotypic differences between sua-CMS and gla-CMS (both share the nuclear of K326). The genetic mechanism of stamen and pistil deformation of sua-CMS is worthy to be further explored.
Down expression of BMADSgenes might be responsible to pistillody ofsua-CMS

According to the ABCDE model for flower development, the floral organ identity is defined by five classes of homeotic genes, named A, B, C, D and E. In many species, genes regulating flowering are highly conserved. All of these homeotic genes encode MADS-box transcription factors, and are extensively involved in the floral transition and floral organ morphogenesis. The class B, C and E genes specify stamens, and class C and E genes specify carpels. Class B MADS-box transcription factors play a key role in homeotic transformation of stamens into carpels, and the deficiency of class B MADS-box causes pistillody in many species. The transcriptomes analysis between sua-CMS line msZhongyan100 (msZY) and its male control Zhongyan100 (ZY) showed that the expression of MADS genes (SPL/NZZ, PI, AG) decreased in msZY. In this study, the expression of five B-class MADS genes, including pMADS1, GLO1, GLO2, pMADS2.1, pMADS2.2 also significantly reduced in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS (MS K326), and the stamen transformed into pistil-like structures. These data suggested that B-class MADS genes were key factors in regulating pistillody of sua-CMS. The transcriptomes analysis of sua-CMS line msZY also presented that abnormal energy metabolism and PCD may underlie the early developmental differences of msZY and ZY anthers. Our data showed that key genes in the flavonoid biosynthesis pathway and decrease of the flavonoid contents might be partially responsible for the pistillody of sua-CMS line MSK326. Mitochondrial genes regulate the expression of class-B MADS-box genes through MRS, and cause pistillody. Therefore, pistillody of sua-CMS may also be regulated by mitochondrial genes through MRS. Moreover, the biological processes underlying CMS or pistillody processes are complex, although the studies have shown that class B MADS-box members are extensively involved in the stamen transition and stamen organ morphogenesis. There are still many other factors that have not yet been discovered, such as how the MRS regulate the expression of MADS-box, and which genes and pathways are targeted and regulated by the MADS to determine pistillody.
Flavonoids are important factors affecting the stamen development ofsua-CMS

Flavonoids, one of the largest groups of plant secondary metabolites, regulate multi-biological processes through interacting with transport and signal transduction pathways, including plant growth, development, reproduction, scavenge ROS and responses to biotic and abiotic stress. Especially, flavonoids perform important functions in male fertility. In present study, CHI, CHS were key genes regulating flavonoid synthesis, and their expression levels reduced significantly in the pistil like structures of sua-CMS. Un-targeted metabolome detection showed that the contents of flavonoids also significantly reduced in the pistil-like structures of sua-CMS (MS K326). These data suggested that flavonoids were closely related to the development of stamens, and insufficient flavonoid contents may lead to the homeotic transformation of stamens into pistil-like structures. The application of external flavonoids on the flower bud of sua-CMS (MS K326) significantly reduced the pistillody ratio, indicating that flavonoids partially regulated pistillody of sua-CMS (MS K326).
Flavonoids may affect the tobacco stamen development through modulating ROS levels

Flavonols modulate the ROS homeostasis through the nonenzymatic antioxidant mechanism and could maintain intermediate levels of ROS related to stress response, pollination, male gametophyte development, pollen germination, and pollen tube growth. In our study, ROS contents were significantly higher in the bud of sua-CMS (MS K326) than that in K326, and reduced after spraying with flavonols (hesperetin), indicating that the flavonoids might regulate pistillody partially through maintaining ROS levels.
ROS burst caused by mitochondrial dysfunction may be related to pistillody

Mitochondria regulates cellular energy metabolism through electron transport chains (ETC). Mitochondrial genome recombination or rearrangement affects the ETC function of mitochondria and leads to CMS in plants. Mitochondrial genomes of sua-CMS(HD), sua-CMS (yy85), sua-CMS (zy90), and other CMS lines of N. tabacum have been reported. Compared with the mitochondrial genome of maintainer line of N. tabacum, sequences of ATP6, COX2, and SDH3 in sua-CMS changed, which might disrupt the normal function of the mitochondrial ETC. This disruption leads to the accumulation of electrons, which can then react with molecular oxygen to form superoxide, a primary ROS. Appropriate ROS level has an important signal transduction function in the cell, while excessive ROS can exacerbate mitochondrial dysfunction and contribute to cellular oxidative stress. We found that ROS content in the flower buds of sua-K326 was significantly higher than K326 and gla-K326, which may be related to the ETC dysfunction in the mitochondrial genome. This increased ROS levels might regulate pistillody through mitochondrial retrograde signaling (MRR). Further work is needed to identify the mitochondrial gene regulating pistillody, and how they affect the mitochondrial function and ROS levels.
Conclusion

sua-CMS (MS K326) exhibits pistillody and pistil malformation, fruits set ratio, fruits and seed weight reduction. Multiple B-class MADS genes are down expressed in the pistil-like structures of MS K326.These genes are key factors in regulating pistillody of sua-CMS. CHI and CHS, key genes regulating flavonoid synthesis are down-expressed, and flavonoids are significantly reduced in the pistil like structures of MS K326. Application of flavonoids reduced the pistillody frequency and ROS levels of MS K326, indicating that flavonoids regulate pistillody of sua-CMS through modulating ROS levels. Our study is of great significance for the seed production of sua-CMS, and provides new insights into understanding the regulatory mechanism of pistillody widely occurred in plants.

passages.text: Meaning in Life as an Outcome of Inpatient or Day-Hospital Psychotherapy for Personality Disorder
ABSTRACT

Psychotherapy may contribute to the experience of meaning in life. This study investigated meaning in life among patients with personality disorders during inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy. Meaning in life was approached from two conceptual perspectives: personality functioning with an emphasis on self-direction and existential psychology. We investigated changes in the sense of meaning in life and accounted for changes in depressive symptoms and identity and interpersonal pathology. Using pre-post measures, Livesley's General Assessment of Personality Disorder, especially, the Lack-of-Meaning-Purpose-and-Direction subscale and Steger's Meaning-in-Life Presence subscale were administered to 75 patients with personality disorders during inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for 8-12 months. Regression models showed that levels of the lack and presence of meaning decreased and increased during treatment, respectively, controlled for changes in depressive symptoms. Decreased identity pathology was significantly associated with changes in the lack or presence of meaning. Meaning in life may act as an outcome variable in intensive psychotherapy for personality disorders. The development of identity and self-direction may restore or create the ability to give life meaning.
Introduction

Issues related to meaning in life (MIL) play explicit or implicit roles in problems among patients seeking psychotherapy (Hill et al. ). MIL is a central issue in both logotherapy (Frankl ) and existential psychotherapy (Yalom ). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, a contemporary mindfulness-based behavior therapy (Hayes ), targets the creation of a valued, meaningful life. MIL is also an important theme in positive psychotherapy (Seligman, Rashid, and Parks ) and the concept of personal recovery among people suffering from severe mental disorders (Leamy et al. ).

In the treatment of personality disorders (PDs), restoring a sense of meaning and purpose in life is also an important aim. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is ultimately about a life worth living (Linehan and Wilks ), especially targeted in later stages of treatment (Liljedahl et al. ). Mentalization in mentalization-based treatment refers to the capacity to create a psychological narrative that integrates one's thoughts, emotions, and intentions, thereby sustaining a coherent and agentive sense of self (Bateman and Fonagy ). The healthy adult mode, a transdiagnostic core concept in schema therapy refers to having a sense of a coherent self and identity and the ability to set and pursue goals (Bach and Bernstein ). Reconstructing and enriching self-narratives or life stories in therapy can provide a sense of purpose and direction (Dimaggio et al. ; Lind, Sharp, and Dunlop ).

This study examined explicitly how the sense of MIL changed during the course of inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for patients with PDs. Studies into MIL demonstrated that the experience of MIL increased after inpatient psychotherapy for patients with depressive, anxiety or somatoform disorders (Volkert et al. ). Recent cross-sectional studies suggested that the therapeutic relationship fostered meaning-making, which lead to better therapy outcome in short-term outpatient person-centered and experiential psychotherapies (Fortems et al. ). Longitudinal research with clients in outpatient open-ended psychodynamic psychotherapy showed similar results, which added that reflectivity regarding MIL was associated with improvements after psychotherapy (Rim, Hill, and Kivlighan ). MIL for patients with PD may be especially worth investigating because a coherent sense of self or identity that provides direction and meaning to their lives may be at stake (Livesley ).
MIL can be approached from personality and existential psychological perspectives.

Regarding MIL as an existential psychological concept, several researchers distinguished three dimensions: (1) having a purpose in life, (2) a life being coherent and making sense, and (3) feeling of significance or mattering (George and Park ; Heintzelman and King ; Martela and Steger ). This concept showed some correspondence with the conceptualization of PD in the Alternative DSM-5 Model of Personality Disorder (AMPD) (American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5 Task Force ) and suggested both an overlap and a distinction.

The AMPD describes "purpose" and "coherence" as part of the personality function indicated as self-direction: pursuit of meaningful and coherent short-term and life goals. Accordingly, Livesley (Livesley and Clarkin ) defines self-direction as an ability to provide personal meaning, goals, and direction to life among other things, as operationalized in the General Assessment of Personality Disorder (GAPD) (Livesley ) questionnaire, which is regarded as a predecessor of the AMPD (Morey et al. ). Purposefulness is more central in the definitions of self-direction, and existential psychological definition of MIL refers to the significance of one's life, ultimate meaning, and purpose.

The AMPD evaluates personality functioning on a continuum. This continuum (operationalized as the Level of Personality Functioning scale) defines severe impairment in self-direction as difficulty in establishing and/or achieving personal goals and experiencing life as meaningless or dangerous. Therefore, dysfunction in self-direction may lead to the conclusion that life is meaningless. MIL can therefore act as an outcome variable, which is related to personality functioning. It is also related to well-being and mental health and considered a necessity in life (Heintzelman and King ).

Following AMPD's description of personality functioning, treatment should aim to ameliorate all maladaptive levels, such as self-pathology (identity and self-direction) and interpersonal pathology (empathy and intimacy). These functions are often intertwined. Striving to attain meaningful goals has been conceptualized as contributing to the coherence of self, identity, meaning, a sense of direction, purpose, agency, and autonomy in life (Livesley and Clarkin ). Purposeful goal pursuit is consistent with the core aspects of identity and may contribute to self-knowledge development (Bronk ). As relationships are a major source of MIL (King and Hicks ), personality functions concerning interpersonal pathology (Livesley ; American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5 Task Force ) may be an influencing factor. Interpersonal pathology can hinder patients with PD from feeling connected with others.

Depressive symptoms have a major correlation with lack of MIL (Volkert et al. ; Steen et al. ). Complaints of depression resemble feelings of worthlessness. Patients with PD experienced lesser meaning and purpose compared with the control group, controlled for depressive complaints (Steen et al. ). Experiencing lack of MIL can occur temporarily or during longer episodes, such as depressive periods. This differs, although often difficult to distinguish from a further enduring way where lack of meaning occurs within the context of personality dysfunction. Whether depression should be regarded as part of PD is another question. Van and Kool  emphasized that depression in patients with PD is a rather coincident disorder than comorbid one. Therefore, we considered the severity and changes in self-reported depressive symptoms to investigate the independent changes occurring in MIL.

Did MIL change during inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy among patients with PD, either from a self-direction perspective, operationalized with the GAPD-LMPD, or from an existential perspective, operationalized with the MLQ Presence, or both?
Did the severity and changes in depressive symptoms affect changes in MIL?
Were changes in identity and interpersonal pathology associated with changes in MIL during inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy among patients with PD?

This naturalistic cohort study focused on the changes in MIL among patients with PD after intensive inpatient and day-hospital psychotherapy. MIL was assessed both pretreatment and posttreatment with two questionnaires that followed the two paradigmatic perspectives: personality function and existential. From a personality functioning perspective, we utilized the GAPD (Livesley ). The lack of meaning, purpose, and direction in life (GAPD-LMPD) received special attention. From an existential perspective, the MIL Questionnaire Presence subscale (MLQ Presence) (Steger et al. ) was used. The latter is most commonly used internationally. This self-report questionnaire relied on subjective, intuitive judgements regarding meaning, similar to other questionnaires. There are numerous possibilities regarding the scarcely verified relationships between these judgements and MIL as purpose, coherence, and significance/mattering (George and Park ; King and Hicks ). This study investigated global meaning from two perspectives. The GAPD-LMPD and MLQ Presence showed a moderately strong correlation in a recent study (Steen et al. ), confirming that these questionnaires did not assess identical constructs. This study examined MIL as a potential outcome variable that has particular relevance for PD patients because it captures a metric related to structural changes in personality over and beyond short-term improvements. Our research questions were as follows:
Methods
Participants

Participants (N = 75) were recruited in 2015-2018 from inpatient and day-hospital PD courses at GGz Centraal, a large regional mental healthcare institute in the Netherlands. All the patients were diagnosed with PD and completed the questionnaires before and after treatment. This naturalistic cohort study contained patients that were willing to participate, before and after treatment (see also Steen et al. ). The estimation was that the majority of patients agreed, creating a consecutive sample. The study involves a completer analysis. Initially 106 patients participated during their assessment period before treatment. Eleven patients never started treatment, four patients dropped out before 2 months, and four other patients were noncompleter. Twelve participants were lost to follow-up. In addition, 57 patients (76%) received inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for 5 and 3 or 4 days per week respectively, both psycho-dynamically oriented, for 9-12 months. The treatment consisted of large group meetings, socio-therapy, group psychotherapy, nonverbal therapies, systemic therapy when possible, and pharmacotherapy when necessary. The remaining 18 (24%) patients received similar day-hospital psychotherapeutic treatment, except for the large group meetings. Their treatments involved mentalization-based or schema-focused oriented psychotherapy for 8-9 months.

PD diagnosis was assessed using structured clinical interviews based on the Dutch version (Weertman, Arntz, and Kerkhofs ) of the DSM-IV-TR Personality Disorders (SCID-II), by trained psychologists with monthly intervision (First et al. ). The most prevalent PDs were borderline (43%), avoidant (30%), and otherwise not specified (25%). Among those with borderline PD, 59% had one or more other PDs. Borderline and avoidant PD occurred in 16% of 75 patients. Other mental disorders were diagnosed and classified clinically according to the DSM-IV-TR. Furthermore, 92% had comorbid disorders, the most frequent being depressive (59%) and anxiety disorders (27%).

The institutional scientific committee authorized data collection. All participants provided written informed consent and received a $7.50 gift certificate for participation. Patients with organic mental disorders, intellectual disability, psychotic disorders, acute crises, or insufficient command of the Dutch language were excluded.
Measurements
GAPD (Livesley ), Authorized Dutch Translation (Berghuis )

This self-reported questionnaire had two main components proposed in Livesley's adaptive failure model: self-pathology and interpersonal pathology. The GAPD aimed to assess different aspects of self and interpersonal functioning, similar to Criterion A of the AMPD (Hentschel and Pukrop ). The GAPD demonstrated favorable psychometric properties in a mixed psychiatric sample (Berghuis et al. ). Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = totally disagree; 5 = totally agree). Self-pathology included items related to the structure of personality (problems of differentiation and integration and consequences of structural problems of the self) and self-direction. Interpersonal dysfunction referred to failure of kinship and societal functioning. The GAPD comprised 19 subscales, eleven about self-pathology, three about self-direction, and four about interpersonal pathology. From a personality function perspective and aligned with the AMPD, the GAPD-LMPD subscale was used to operationalize lack of MIL. This subscale included four items: (1) nothing that I do seems to have much purpose, (2) I drift through life without a clear sense of direction, (3) my life seems to have little meaning, and (4) most of the time, I feel that what I do is meaningful and valuable (reverse item). In a previous study, Cronbach's alphas were 0.73 and 0.86 in a group of mental healthcare patients with PD and non-PD and convenience sample, respectively (Steen, Berghuis, and Braam ). The GAPD was part of the regular assessment procedure.
Meaning in Life Questionnaire (MLQ) (Steger et al. )

This 10-item self-reported questionnaire contained two 5-item scales that measured the Presence of and Search for MIL. The presence of meaning subscale measured people's appraisals of meaning and purpose in their lives ("I have discovered a satisfying life purpose"). One reverse item measured a lack of meaning: "My life has no clear purpose." Responses were rated on a 7-point scale (1 = absolutely untrue; 7 = absolutely true). Previous research supported the scale's internal consistency, stability, and the structural, convergent, and discriminant validity (Steger et al. ). Cronbach's alpha for the MLQ Presence scale in this study was 0.86.
Symptom Checklist-90-Revised (SCL-90-R) (Derogatis and Lazarus ), Dutch translation (Arrindell and Ettema )

This scale evaluated nine symptom dimensions: somatization, obsessive-compulsive, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, hostility, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation, and psychoticism. We utilized the depression dimension with 16 items scored on a 5-point scale (0 = not at all; 4 = extremely). The SCL-90-R was an internationally validated, reliable questionnaire with good psychometric properties. This checklist was part of the assessment procedure.
Data Analysis

First, the demographic characteristics and mean scores of the MLQ Presence, GAPD-LMPD, GAPD SP 1-12 (Subscale Self Pathology scales 1-12, without the self-directedness subscales 13-15, GAPD IP (Subscale Interpersonal Pathology), and SCL-90-R depression were described. Effect sizes (Cohen's d pre-post) were computed for each variable. We examined the pretreatment and posttreatment changes in the two variables regarding MIL (GAPD-LMPD and MLQ Presence) and regressed the change score on a constant only, similar to a one-sample t-test. Subsequently, we used two separate univariate regression models for each variable. The first univariate model regressed the change in MIL on (centered) pretreatment depression severity score (DSS) measured using the SCL-90-R depression subscale, which indicated how the change related to the baseline depression severity self-report score. The second univariate model regressed the change in MIL on changes in DSS (using the SCL-90-R Depression score), which indicated how the changes were related to change in DSS. The intercept indicated the mean change in meaning of life for patients without changes in DSSs.

In the third model, we regressed the change in the GAPD-LMPD and MLQ Presence on the pre-post change in the sum score of the first 12 scales of the GAPD (GAPD-SP1-12) that pertained to self-pathology, without the sum score of the GAPD self-directedness scales 13-15. Finally, in the fourth model, we regressed the change in the GAPD-LMPD and MLQ Presence on the pre-post change in GAPD Interpersonal Pathology (GAPD-IP), which was the sum scores of the scales 16-19. Analyses were conducted using SPSS 28.0.
Results

Table 1 presents the participants' characters. The pre-post effect size was large for the MLQ Presence (Cohen's d = 0.8), GAPD-LMPD (Cohen's d = -1.3), GAPD SP 1-12 (Cohen's d = -1.2), and SCL-90-R depression (Cohen's d = -1.3) and medium for GAPD IP (Cohen's d = -0.5).A paired samples t-test (Table 2, Model A0) showed a statistically significant pre-post decrease in lack of MIL, with a large within-group effect. In Model A1, we observed a significant decrease in the GAPD-LMPD after treatment, adjusted for pretreatment DSS.

In Model A2, we observed a decrease in the mean GAPD-LMPD, irrespective of a pre-post change in depression severity. The decrease in the GAPD-LMPD scores was significantly larger when the DSS further decreased (negative values of the pre-post change in DSS implied a decrease in DSS).

Model A3 showed a strong association between pre-post change in the GAPD-LMPD and other GAPD self-pathology scales and GADP-SP1-12. Furthermore, the pre-post change in the GAPD-LMPD was small and not statistically significant, controlled for pre-post change in the other GAPD self-pathology scales. Pre-post changes in the GAPD-SP1-12 showed a highly significant positive correlation with changes in the GAPD-LMPD. Finally, model A4 showed a moderate to strong association between pre-post change in the GAPD-LMPD and GADP-IP. Furthermore, the pre-post change in the GAPD-LMPD was statistically significant, irrespective of pre-post changes in the GAPD-IP. These pre-post changes in the GAPD-IP showed a highly significant positive association with changes in the GAPD-LMPD.

Table 2 presents the results for the MLQ Presence (Model B0). The t-test showed a statistically significant pre-post difference, with a large within-group effect size of Cohen's d = 0.8. The MLQ Presence (Model B1) showed that the mean increase after treatment was not significantly affected by pretreatment DSSs. Model B2 showed a mean increase in MLQ Presence after inclusion of the DSS pre-post change scores. These DSS pre-post changes showed an inverse and highly significant positive association with changes in the MLQ Presence score.

Model B3 showed a strong association between pre-post change in MLQ Presence and GADP-SP1-12. In addition, the pre-post change in MLQ Presence was small and not statistically significant after pre-post change in the GAPD-SP1-12 was included in the model. These pre-post changes in the GAPD-SP1-12 showed a highly significant and inverse association with changes in MLQ Presence.

Finally, model B4 showed a moderate association (beta = -0.35) between the pre-post change in MLQ Presence and the GADP-IP. The pre-post change in MLQ Presence was statistically significant even after the pre-post change in the GAPD-IP was included. The pre-post change in the GAPD-IP showed a significant inverse association with MLQ Presence.
Discussion

Several studies supported the assumption that the sense of MIL increased during psychotherapy, even if it did not specifically focus on it (Volkert et al. ; Fortems et al. ; Rim, Hill, and Kivlighan ). Regarding PD, psychotherapy may influence personality dysfunctions, such as a lack of self-direction, which was defined as the pursuit of coherent and meaningful short- and long-term goals in the AMPD (American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5 Task Force ) and Livesley's adaptive failure model (Livesley ). Psychotherapy may also influence existential meaning, which was conceptualized as having a purpose in life, sense of coherence, and sense of significance or mattering (George and Park ; Martela and Steger ; King and Hicks ). To our best knowledge, comparison of these two perspectives over the naturalistic course of inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for PD is a novel approach. Our research might contribute to the accumulation of evidence that MIL is an indicator of well-being and mental health (Steger ).

Our first research question was whether MIL changed during inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for patients with PD, either from a self-direction perspective operationalized with the GAPD-LMPD or an existential perspective operationalized with the MLQ Presence or both. The results showed that levels of the lack and existential presence of MIL as part of a personality function decreased and increased, respectively. This effect persisted, adjusted for gradual change in depressive symptoms.

These results indicated that psycho-dynamically oriented, mentalization-based, and schema-focused inpatient or day-hospital psychotherapy for PDs was likely to affect MIL from both perspectives. The GAPD-LMPD and MLQ Presence differed slightly. The GAPD-LMPD assessed items that pertained to the lack of self-direction, which was understood as purposefulness. Restoring personality functions could restore the ability to create meaning, as a meaning framework (Sharp and Wall ) or could be regarded as an antecedent factor for existential meaning (King and Hicks ). The MLQ Presence aimed at one's life, on understanding the meaning of one's life, its significance, and one's life purpose. Alternatively, as our findings could not disregard causal relationships, the restoration of morale, which is a common outcome psychotherapy (Frank and Frank ), could lead to better personality functioning.

The second research question concerned the expected influence of (changes in) depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms also decreased and were significantly associated with the abovementioned changes in MIL from both perspectives. Furthermore, Remmers et al.  found that losing a felt sense of meaning was related to depression and personality functioning, which indicated that existential crisis could be of transdiagnostic relevance.

The third research question was whether changes in identity and interpersonal pathology were associated with changes in MIL. A decrease in the GAPD identity pathology scales showed significant associations with decreased levels of lack of meaning and increased levels of presence of meaning. No change in the GAPD identity scales also indicated significant change in MIL from both perspectives. Self-worth and personal identity precede a satisfying sense of life meaning (Yalom ). Hence, self was an antecedent factor in MIL (King and Hicks ). The pre-post large effect size of the GAPD-LMPD and the GAPD identity scales and the medium effect size of the GAPD interpersonal scales are in itself indicative of a clinically significant change, as they exceed more than half a standard deviation change (Norman, Sloan, and Wyrwich ).

Identity and self-direction were not distinct entities; however, they were interacting structures and processes that formed an organized system, the self (Livesley ). In the AMPD and Livesley's models, self-pathology consisted of two components: identity and self-direction. Self-direction was more of an ability and part of the total characteristics of a person as were identity characteristics (Glas ). However, identity contained dynamic and temporal elements, such as relating to oneself, being oneself, and telling one's story, and one's narrative identity (McAdams ; Ricoeur ). In being oneself, identity is not a structure but rather who one is and how one deals with life, others, and oneself (Glas ; Ricoeur ; Glas ).

Although the concepts of identity and MIL originated from theoretical systems grounded in different philosophical perspectives, both offered a sense of direction: to know who one was and who one wanted to become (Waterman ). MIL was indeed associated with psychotherapy-related identity aimed as authenticity (Sutton ) and a true self-concept (Schlegel et al. ).

The second part of this research question was whether changes in interpersonal pathology were related to changes in MIL. Change in the interpersonal GAPD scales was significantly associated with decreased levels of lack of meaning and increased levels of presence of meaning. Improving connectedness may lead to better social relationships, a major source of meaning (Glaw et al. ).

Examining the existential concept of MIL that consisted of a sense of purpose, coherence, and significance/mattering may clarify why psychotherapy for PD "worked." A sense of purpose, as part of self-direction, related to motivational strategies and goal-directedness. Coherence may be due to the reconstruction of a more coherent life story, a narrative identity, providing unity, meaning, and purpose to life (McAdams ). Reflective functioning in psycho-dynamically oriented psychotherapy was related to coherence as comprehensibility to understanding oneself.

The results suggested that personality functioning and existential meaning were examined as distinct entities; however, they cannot be separated in therapy. Further research is required on the co-occurrence of PD, existential meaning, and depressive symptoms as possibly intertwined phenomena. The third facet of existential MIL was regarding significance, life's inherent value, and experience of having a life worth living. Living a life worth is often the hardest part in patients with severe PD. "Reasons for living" was a treatment strategy for suicidality, a common feature in patients with borderline PD (Linehan et al.). The goal of DBT was "not only helping patients to survive but also to build a life worth living" (Lynch et al. , 183), the latter also being the title of Linehan's memoir (Linehan ). However, operationalizing "significance" was not covered by theoretical approaches employed in this study.

This study had several limitations. Our study is primarily a preliminary study into MIL due to its naturalistic course. Our study failed to include a control group. Therefore, we cannot state that the positive changes were solely due to the treatment. However, other studies on the improvement of personality functioning as a therapeutic outcome also utilized pre-post measures (Kraus et al. ; Leichsenring et al. ). Our study also failed to include follow-up measurements. Our research questions focused on whether the effects on meaning from an existential perspective and from a personality functioning perspective could be measured immediately after the designated treatment duration. We also did not include other (observer rated) outcome measures, such as global suffering, functioning and social adjustments. A last limitation is that we utilized part of the assessment procedure measures, such as the SCL-90-R, and therefore, we selected the depression subscale for depressive symptom severity, instead of a specific measure.

Further research into MIL addressing these limitations is required to determine whether specific meaning-centered interventions (Vos et al. ; Vos and Vitali ) enhanced MIL in patients with PD. Steger  identified five major meaning-making interventions. First, consciousness: to develop tools to notice, reflect, and create meaning from experiences. Second, time: to utilize and integrate past, present, and future. Third, doing: to intentionally live a purpose, toward valued aims. Fourth, self: to explore, understand, and embrace an authentic self. Last: connecting and engaging with others. These interventions were often part of intensive psychotherapy for personality dysfunction and PD, although the extent and explicitness may differ. In addition, interventions to develop identity and self-direction may restore the ability to create MIL among patients with PD.

We are inclined to separate personality from the existential dimension of being in the world. However, this may be artificial as MIL as an experience was closely associated with both personality and existence as well as self-pathology. Therefore, MIL may be an important outcome variable in psychotherapeutic treatment for PD, linking personality functioning to existential issues.
